#3619. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3618. Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained: Where The Franchise Goes From Here

Full spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero" follow.

For the longest time in the character's 72-year history, the "Godzilla" films were surprisingly light on continuity. During the Showa era films produced by Toho Studios during the 1950s through the 1970s, the most common recurring characters in the movies were the kaiju themselves. When the Heisei era occurred between 1984 and 1996, they established a continuity that was a bit more contiguous, but not much. The Millennium era became even more piecemeal continuity-wise, with most entries using the original 1954 "Godzilla" as a starting point but erasing everything else until the latest film (similar to how the "Halloween" franchise continuity has operated before). Even the MonsterVerse films produced by Legendary Pictures function most similarly to the Heisei era in terms of continuity, while Toho's 2016 "Shin Godzilla" is basically a one-shot.

All of this is to say that the "Godzilla" franchise is wildly unpredictable where canon is concerned, with each film or groups of films essentially treating it piecemeal. It's exceedingly rare that a true sequel has been made to a "Godzilla" film in the past, where a prior movie's cast and filmmakers have returned for a second round. That milestone has finally been achieved with "Godzilla Minus Zero."

The movie is an unabashed sequel to 2023's "Godzilla Minus One," as it's once again written and directed by Takashi Yamazaki. As such, it's a beautifully rich experience previously unseen in most "Godzilla" movies, one which builds from its predecessor in a big way. "Minus Zero" isn't just another "Godzilla" adventure, but a movie which continues the "Minus" series' character arcs and themes, and its emotional, somewhat cliffhanger-style conclusion indicates that the story may not be over yet.

"Godzilla Minus One" takes place between 1945 and 1947, during the immediate aftermath of World War II. Japan's loss of the war has left it hurting in more ways than one, with the country having to muddle through dire straits both physical and emotional. This is represented by the ensemble of characters we meet, chief among them Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), a kamikaze pilot who deserts his suicidal duty, Noriko Ōishi (Minami Hamabe), a woman who takes it upon herself to rescue and raise an orphan girl, Akiko (Sae Nagatani), and Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), a Naval weapons engineer.

All three adults come to view the superpowered creature Godzilla as emblematic of their personal struggles. For Noda, Godzilla must be stopped for Japan to have a future. For Noriko, Godzilla is something to be survived. For Shikishima, Godzilla is the personification of his guilt, as well as a force of death and destruction who must be vanquished.

After Noriko's apparent demise during a Godzilla attack on Ginza, Noda spearheads a civilian-run mission in which a couple of Navy destroyers will alternately sink and raise Godzilla at dangerous speeds. As a failsafe, Shikishima has volunteered to fly one of the last available Shinden fighters to lure Godzilla out to sea. However, his real plan is to fly the plane, loaded with explosives, directly into Godzilla's mouth. He does so, but uses an ejection seat to escape at the last minute, proving he's overcome his guilt and has decided to live. Following the Godzilla victory, Shikishima learns that Noriko has in fact survived, and he and Akiko go to visit her in the hospital. As Noriko tearfully reunites with her new family, a mysterious black mark on her neck shimmers.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" picks up in 1949, when Noda is informed of another giant monster attacking Japan: Ghidorah. As Noda and his new advisor, meterologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), plan to kill Ghidorah with lightning, Noda asks Shikishima for help. Shikishima tries to stay out of the battle for the sake of his now-wife Noriko and adopted daughter Akiko, especially as he and Noriko are the only ones who know that she survived Ginza due to being infected with Godzilla's cells, which might lead to her death soon.

Yet when Ghidorah survives the initial attack and a now-regenerated Godzilla reappears, Noda and biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), a survivor of the Hiroshima bombing, decide the best plan is to lure Godzilla and Ghidorah into a deathmatch fight, with the humans killing the victor. To do this, Murakami has a device which means only Noriko and her G cells can "call" Godzilla.

Shikishima and Noriko agree to the plan, unaware that Murakami intends to later use Noriko as a way to get revenge on the USA. Godzilla and Ghidorah fight in Ginza, and the former eventually triumphs, though at the expense of Noda's life. When the Japanese army gives orders that Godzilla is not to be killed, Shikishima and Noriko mutiny against Murakami. However, Murakami reveals that Noda recently convinced him of the error of his ways, and the couple are allowed to escape while the scientist destroys his machine and his work.

Unfortunately, Murakami's good deed is punished when the US army arrests him. Meanwhile, Shikishima and Noriko try to abandon Akiko, knowing they're doomed to a life on the run from the authorities. Yet they ultimately can't leave her behind, and ride off as a family to an uncertain future.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is a true second chapter in a continuing story. This is a fairly unprecedented occurrence in the Godzilla franchise, not just in the way the returning characters are built upon and expanded, but also in the way Takashi Yamazaki continues the themes from "Minus One." Rather than jumping ahead in time too far, "Minus Zero" is still a story of post-war Japan, and nowhere is this more evident than in Kanji Murakami's character.

Although Godzilla is shifted toward a more heroic light, as has happened many times over the franchise, he's still presented as morally dubious. If, in "Minus One," Godzilla stood for the sins of the Japanese (if not all humanity) come to punish them, "Minus Zero" looks at Godzilla as the country's answer to the atomic bomb: a destructive and ultimately uncontrollable weapon which should only be used as a last resort, if ever.

In addition to the war allegory, "Godzilla Minus Zero" takes the characters of "Minus One" beyond their absolution in that film. Much of "Minus Zero" concerns whether the happy (or relatively happy) future the survivors of that movie fought so hard for can even happen, as everything from the Ghidorah attacks to the potentially deadly G Cells in Noriko's body appears like an insurmountable threat. Yet while unfortunate consequences are unavoidable, Yamazaki's optimism ultimately shines through, especially in the way the bonds between the characters mean that all hope is never lost. Even the supporting cast from "Minus One," though given smaller roles here, contribute to this theme. The implication is that Japan, if not humanity, can have a bright future if everyone supports each other and serves their better natures rather than being selfish or hateful.

If "Godzilla Minus Zero" were to conclude the "Minus" continuity, then both "Godzilla Minus One" and "Minus Zero" would serve as a fully satisfying tale. Still, Takashi Yamazaki does leave "Minus Zero" on several cliffhangers, or at least unresolved questions. The ending leaves the ultimate fate of many characters uncertain, chief among them Murakami and the Shikishima family. In the case of the former, it seems likely that the US army intend to make Murakami work for them to get Godzilla under American control.

In the case of the latter, the Shikishimas are now going to be on the run, and it's unclear what their plan is to evade the government(s). It's neat how these films have set up so much good material with the human characters that there's enough interest in what happens to them before one even considers the kaiju.

But oh, the giant monsters! We cannot forget about them. Now that Yamazaki has introduced Ghidorah, the door is open for any other Toho-verse kaiju to turn up. In terms of the themes that the "Minus" films are dealing with, it would feel appropriate for other heavily allegorical beasts like Rodan or Hedorah to make their appearance. Although the MonsterVerse's "Godzilla vs. Kong" recently used Mechagodzilla as humanity's warmongering response to Godzilla, such a characterization would fit snugly into the "Minus" films, too. And, while "Minus Zero" only contains a fantasy sequence of Godzilla attacking NYC, there's the chance that the action could expand beyond Japan for real. While it's not clear whether there will be another "Minus" film at all yet, there's certainly no dearth of possibilities for one to explore.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3617. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City.

#3616. Right Now Is the Perfect Time to Play the Quietly Best Yakuza Spinoff

When Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name was released in 2023, the Yakuza series was in a strange position. The team at Sega's Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio was gearing up to give a heroic sendoff to longtime protagonist Kazuma Kiryu. They had big plans for 2024's Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth to pass the torch to a new main character. But Yakuza had unexpectedly become bigger than ever outside Japan, thanks largely to the viral success of Yakuza 0 throughout the late 2010s and early 2020s. The fans demanded more Kiryu, not less. And developer Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio rose to the occasion with The Man Who Erased His Name, an interquel that depicts his lonely years in exile after the events of Yakuza 6.

"We could have just told of Kiryu’s past through a thirty-minute interlude as part of Like a Dragon 8 [Infinite Wealth], but we decided it would be a lot more interesting as a game of its own, which is how the project came to be," series producer Masayoshi Yokoyama told Automaton in October 2023. "Though this meant having a whole extra game to make, it still uses the same engine, so we thought 'It’s not like we have to make it from scratch,' and decided to go with it. In the end, it took us about half a year to make it."

While this doesn't sound all that promising, The Man Who Erased His Name delivers some of the series' all-time best storytelling and character work. With Japan's criminal underworld forever changed after a decades-long government conspiracy comes to light inYakuza 6, Kiryu must work with the Daidoji Clan, a shadowy organization of spies and fixers. Our hero knows a bit too much about the connections between the government, police, and organized crime, so the Daidoji threaten his family to ensure he plays along. Armed with identity-concealing sunglasses and magic cigarettes, Kiryu assumes the identity of the secret agent Joryu after faking his own death.

While he's on the clock, Joryu's dishing out pain to dozens of goons at a time. When he's not, Kiryu is adrift and miserable, isolated from everyone he's ever cared about. Yakuza players will be accustomed to seeing Kiryu with the odds stacked against him, but this is a gloomy rock bottom like never before. He spends much of his time meditating in a buddhist temple or smoking countless cigarettes. It's probably best enjoyed if you've played at least one other game in the series, but if you manage to make it through the ending of The Man Who Erased His Name without shedding a tear, you're made of solid stone.

Compared to the mainline Yakuza games, The Man Who Erased His Name is a brief, compact experience — just 15-20 hours compared to the usual 60+. You'll spend most of your time in the familiar Sotenbori district of Osaka, a staple location of the series, as well as the Isezaki Ijincho district of Yokohama from Like a Dragon and Infinite Wealth. The sidequel also adds a new location, the floating vice ship known as the Castle, which features a fighting arena, a cabaret club, Pocket Circuit racing, and the inevitable karaoke.

Best of all, The Man Who Erased His Name is significantly lowered-price on the PlayStation Store right now, discounted from $49.99 to $9.99. The sale runs through Nov. 21. The game is also available on Windows PC and Xbox Series X.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

I don’t know this light. In memory, it is a brighter, warmer sun that pours over skin that isn’t mine, honing kaleidoscopic fragrances carried upon a soft breeze. I search for the names of these scents, but they elude me. Same goes for the greenery, dew kissed and glistening, a rainbow of flowers blossoming within its branches. It’s a pleasant picture, this remembrance that isn’t mine, experienced gods know where, a thousand leagues away and borne across immeasurable stretches of land and sea. I hold it as long as I can before reality begins to gnaw again at its lacerated edges, rending it apart.

The Cathedral of the Enduring Flame is gone. Good riddance, except I sense its destruction like my own flesh and blood—fractured, scattered, spilled. That empty space where the structure used to stand is nothing but smoking ruins, which, if I had to guess, is still spitting up the occasional dead body or two. Fires continue to smolder beneath the worst of it, stubborn embers in the rubble that refuse to go out.

The scale of destruction presses down on the secluded chamber where I sit quietly in the dark, entombed beneath what used to be one of the grandest structures in the Devoted Lands. For the hundredth time—or maybe the thousandth, who’s counting?—I press the point of one sickle to the pad of my thumb. A bead of blood wells up, round as the room, black as obsidian. I shouldn’t be able to see it at all. There are no oil lamps here, not a speck of illumination that reaches this deep in the earth, despite the fresh fissures in the stones above. And yet, here we are. The bead grows fat as an overfed tick and ruptures, drawing a dark line down to my palm. I lick it away. Salt. A faint metallic tanginess. Nothing new or unfamiliar. Not now, nor the countless times I’ve checked before. When I pull the digit back, the wound is gone, nothing left to show it was there, save for a faint sheen of tinted spit.

“Not sure what I expected.” I speak aloud, though I don’t need to, the statement flattened by the dense silence. “A little zip. A hint of spice. Something.”

No answer. Only the understanding. Of us.

It’s been days since Osiron’s attack, maybe a week. Time has taken on a weird texture, stretching like taffy before snapping back into place, rarely with the definition it should have. Oh, the jagged, shattered hours that followed my—our almost deaths are clear enough. Digging out from beneath the Cathedral, picking through the debris on a hunt for survivors, all the while sensing the fading glow of my Chosen—my brethren, beneath the devastation. The few left alive, anyway. It was an effective blow. Desperate and downright dirty, but effective. Gotta give Osiron that.

The Whisperer took their hits too, of course. The foul rankness of their followers’ remains still lingers in my nostrils, what was left of them deteriorated and barely identifiable following their consumption of a dead god’s blood in their effort to topple me.

Fuck. I do not love this feeling. This tangled, snake-pit sensation of being myself and not, someone else and not. Of you, Tempestra, buzzing around the peripheries of my mind. Not that I really knew what to expect when I let you wriggle in. I suppose I should be thankful you held to your promise not to slurp my consciousness down like an oyster from its shell, though I don’t know if it’s better or worse that you’ve receded to lick the divine wounds left after you healed my physical ones. Especially since I can’t quite shake the feeling of your breath against my neck, your shadow brushing across mine. Or the visions that keep rising to the surface, some other avatar’s stolen memories that you’ve kept like tacky little trinkets, entertaining as they are.

Worst of all is the awareness of that new thing, out there somewhere, clothed in its stolen body. Faint but constant, a threat and a taunt and an ache I cannot quiet. That’s a little bit of both of us, though, the desire to hunt down the still-fragile creature Osiron midwifed into this world. I keep wondering if the Whisperer regrets their strange gamble now. You and I’d both be dead as dead can be if the Whisperer had remembered an old lesson instead of trying to learn a new one: Never turn your back on a foe, no matter how defeated they seem.

I’ve grown accustomed to not getting one, outside of the occasional understanding of something I had little knowledge of before. A broadening of my mind, as if I opened a door at the back of a tiny library only to find a thousand more like it, every shelf filled to overflowing with tomes. To think all of it might have disappeared with Tempestra’s demise, which, until recently, was what I’d wanted more than anything. A wish that would have been fulfilled—at the acceptable price of my own expiration—if not for Osiron’s posturing miscalculation.

I wanted to go after him immediately. Tried to. We were only hours behind, and Osiron didn’t exactly escape unscathed. Between our conflict and the summoning of a new deity, the Whisperer’s power had been heavily spent. They were weak. Vulnerable.

Another confrontation so soon is . . . ill-advised. All the explanation I got. A feeble position for the supposedly most powerful being in existence to take, but then again, the only reason that being still managed the in existence part was me. My upgrade to divine avatar brought a fresh surge of power, but apparently it was short-lived. So: Rest. Recover. Rescue who could be rescued from the remains of the Cathedral and then . . .

I ignore them, as I have a dozen times before. They’re barely audible to begin with, a faint series of thumps beyond the thick door of the underground chamber where a goddess once invited two of their Chosen to show off a crucial, closely held secret. What remains of that secret, the reliquary that I—that they’d kept hidden all these years, still sits on a pillar at the center of the room, its singular piece of decor. I’ve thought about smashing it about as many times as I’ve pricked my finger. What it contains is considered by most to be a gift rather than a curse—me, being part of the minority—but it’s an unwelcome reminder. Of what was forced upon me. Of not being cautious enough to ensure the rest had been destroyed, or realizing that the Whisperer still lived and, because of that deception, Osiron—weak, wiggling, manipulative creature that they are and always have been—was able to—

Nope. Not following that path of thought again, Tempestra. That’s yours, not mine.

“Shit . . .” They aren’t going to go away this time.

Seclusion was our little compromise. A near frenzy followed the destruction of the Cathedral, the people of the city of Lumeris frantic to understand what had happened, who had been behind the attack, what the Goddess (in their fresh, new flesh) was going to do, and on and on and on and on . . .

No, thanks. If we couldn’t go after Osiron and Nolan, if we absolutely needed time to restore ourselves, I wasn’t about to do it amid all that nonsense. Especially on my mostly lonesome. Should have known there’s no hiding away forever, though. Our devoted are coming—yet another thing my newly divine senses kept flagging. Countless pilgrims are descending like locusts on Lumeris, the city filling more and more as the days pass. Facing that gathering horde was always an inevitability.

Not to mention, I’m beginning to get hungry.

Can’t lie, that’s a bit of a rub. I know—the way I know too many new things—that my body doesn’t need food and water in the same way it did when I was sans Goddess, but it’s still a body of flesh and blood and bile and piss. It still requires some tending. A heartier plant than before, maybe, but subject to certain bounds of its nature, as all things are. I push myself up from the floor, frame aching with the reminder that I haven’t moved in what—a day? Two? The door lies directly across from me. There’s no handle or keyhole. Only me. I make my way over, hesitating right before I touch the iron-studded wood.

Ugh. There’s a whole gaggle of Chosen on the other side of it. Who I’d much prefer to go on ignoring, but before I can lock in that decision, the part of me that’s not me lays our palm on the door. A clunking noise follows, and it opens.

After all my time in the pitch-black, the brightness of their oil lamps should have blinded me, even briefly. Instead, I discover a crystal-clear tableau of what currently makes up the senior leadership of the Flame Goddess’s Orders.

To call them dregs would be rude. Probably not rude enough to make them fuck off, though.

So many of my Chosen—dammit, my brethren—were killed in Osiron’s attack. Enough that I didn’t bother overseeing their funerary preparations before we “excused” ourselves. They weren’t the only losses either. Over the past few days a feeling has come from time to time, the sensation of a candle being blown out somewhere far away. I do not know names, cannot picture faces, but we feel them nonetheless.

You’ve felt most of them, haven’t you, Tempestra? The deaths of your Chosen, even the ones shuffled away and abandoned in some forgotten corner of your lands. And yet, I’ve watched you cry over their bodies. Does that affection only carry to the city limits, or do you consider a certain amount of attrition by murder the cost of doing divine business?

And what the hell do the ones in front of us want now?

Five nervous figures wait for me to give them permission to speak. Their features sway between a mélange of emotions, awe and fear and— worst of all—love. They are not the cream of the crop, but they’re what’s left: Rallo, my new High Arbiter, fully white-eyed and ancient enough to be panting from the trip down here; Prior Superior Krestor, scruffy in a way that makes me think of a hound dog; High Cleric of the Blood Emmeric, fervor pouring from him in the most irritating way possible; my new Bellator Prime, Ysell, appropriately stoic but an odd duck among her Order, the only one without command of a legion.

And last but not least, my handpicked, brand-spanking-new Executrix.

Morgan probably doesn’t realize how she winces slightly upon seeing me, her eyes tightening as she stares at her old rival turned Goddess. But, oh, I catch it, that faint reaction to the flesh she’d known our whole lives (Innara) now suddenly become Lys, whom she’s hated more or less from our first day together in the Dawn Cloister. I keep my expression blank especially for her, as tranquil as a goddess should be. Tempestra might be mostly tucked away catching their breath, but what fun is it if Morgan knows that?

“What do you need?” Benevolent entity that I’m supposed to be, I opt for a gentle approach, speaking in the way I remember Tempestra- Innara addressing us: quiet, calm, cool. All light, no fire. “I did not wish to be disturbed.”

Despite my effort, they all wince a bit at that.

Except Bellator Ysell. She steps forward, dipping her head respectfully. “We are sorry to disturb you, Goddess. But crowds have continued to gather outside the wall of the Cathedral complex, and they are becoming . . . unsettled.” When I don’t press for an explanation, she continues awkwardly. “There are . . . rumors circulating.”

“Distressing ones,” Prior Superior Krestor jumps in, spitting a little in his excitement to contribute. “Foul notions, about the extinguishing of the Flame, the return of the dead gods, of... of the...”

“Of the Whisperer,” I finish. The divine power in me surges briefly, angry at the threat that shouldn’t be a threat. At the god who was supposed to be dead.

“Our clerics are working hard to quell the gossip,” offers High Cleric of the Blood Emmeric, “as well as reassure the devoted that their Goddess not only lives, but thrives in their newly appointed avatar. That the Flame burns as brightly as ever.”

A gross overstatement, if we’re being honest. But I nod, understanding, because none of them would be here right now if the tales being spun by the clerics were being swallowed. I know what they are asking of me.

They part as I move forward, taking the lead of our little party as we traverse the tunnels that coil beneath the Cathedral complex. These remained mostly untouched by the destruction above, though I observe cracks that weren’t there before, fresh weaknesses in the stone and mortar. Our path is indirect, winding through the safest passages and up into what halls still stand before reaching open air. Once there, a field of shattered glass and crumbled stone spreads out before us.

Regret and sorrow suddenly fill me, not all of it Tempestra’s. I hated the Cathedral, its stuffy eaves and buttresses and the stupid, spindly tower above it, where a flame once burned day and night as a beacon to pilgrims. It was, for me, a structural reminder of my divine cage—a place where I was victim, murderer, and then victim again. But it was beautiful too. The hands of a thousand artisans had touched it over the centuries, driven by deep devotion. A face stares up from the debris: the remains of one of the countless statues of past Chosen that once lined the Cathedral’s corridors. Positioned as it is, the features on the broken head appear imploring, but also blank. Cold. And too reminiscent of the other faces that looked out of the rubble. I wave a hand. The nose crumbles; the eyes and lips disappear, as if sanded away. I don’t check to see if my Chosen have noticed my little trick, but I feel at least one pair of eyes piercing my back.

Avatar or Lys, it’s hard to ignore Morgan’s stare.

But that sensation fades beneath another that’s growing stronger with each passing moment, the very reason I opted to hide us in the reliquary chamber, when leadership was the expected course. The Cathedral is destroyed. A dead god has returned. Obviously the Flame’s followers are more than a little concerned. I feel their fears radiating, thickening the air as I pick my way through gardens and across the plazas, until we reach the great gate that marks the boundary between the Cathedral complex and the decadent, sprawling city of Lumeris below. The doors survived, though I can see why my senior advisors are getting antsy about that being a continuing condition.

The crowds have come. Countless thousands fill every open space as people press to get closer, attempting to see the travesty that has occurred with their own eyes. This ocean of individuals floods the city streets, flowing out of view like tributary rivers. Despite their number, the gathered are mostly silent, clutching their reveries— pendant-sized representations of the Flame rendered in crystal or gold or even plain wood—emitting only a low buzz of what might be prayer, but also might be questions and gossip that tread dangerously close to blasphemy.

That all disappears the moment we step into view. A shocked hush falls, short-lived as a swell of sound rises on its heels, turning quickly to a roar—cries of excitement and relief and the ecstasy of the Goddess’s reappearance. A rare treat: For the majority of living memory, the Flame has taken its audiences within the Cathedral, displayed only to a lucky few. Now, that stingy tradition is set aside in favor of some desperately needed proof of life. It’s almost overwhelming, the sheer sense of them all. Their confusion and uncertainty pours over and through me, infused with apprehension, desire, and . . .

I see the Arbiters. A trio, set apart from the crowd, still as marble pillars in their cold white cassocks. To one side of them a mixture of Cathedral and city guards are stationed—practically toylike in armor that has, until very recently, been mostly ceremonial—surrounding a cluster of figures on their knees, chained to one another. All are slumped forward and looking . . . well, not much better than what’s been dragged out from beneath the Cathedral ruins. The pungent tang of congealed blood and emptied bladders reaches me.

There’s that breath on my neck again. I turn to Morgan. “Were you going to mention this? Or is a bunch of beat-to-hell strangers the traditional ‘welcome to godhood’ gift?”

“Heretics,” my Executrix spits, failing to round the curtness off the word. Which she must realize, given the embarrassed flush that touches her cheeks. “While you’ve been . . . communing, we’ve been combing the city, searching for any traitors operating in secret.” How industrious of my new senior Chosen.

Rallo hobbles over. “They have yet to be judged, Goddess, but the evidence is unquestionable. They are guilty and thus deserving of whatever punishment you deem appropriate.”

I’m almost impressed by how my Chosen have blindsided me. Not that they’d see it that way. No, excluding Morgan and Ysell, they look as pleased as cats who have dumped a chewed-up mouse at my feet. An offering to their new avatar, their rekindled Flame.

The bitter laugh that wells in my throat nearly escapes. Whatever punishment that I “deem appropriate.” Any twisted, horrible, cruel sentence I’m in the mood for, so long as it serves to make an example of these unlucky folks. I might have them thrown into some moldy, window less, and vermin-filled prison to slowly rot. Or instruct Morgan to carve their innards from them, piece by piece, one victim at a time. But those choices, while fitting, would not offer the satisfaction desired by my devoted audience. As thousands of eyes stare, expectant and eager, I can’t pretend I don’t understand exactly what is being asked of me.

And the punishment for heresy is to burn.

#3610. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3608. Magic's Star Trek Already Feels a Lot More Frustrating than Reality Fracture

MTG Star Trek Limited is not as smooth as Reality Fracture

A mere six weeks have passed since the release of Reality Fracture, one of the best-received Magic: The Gathering sets in recent years, and players are already primed to enter warp speed with Star Trek. Universes Beyond sets always get their fair share of criticism, and while it’s understandable that not every Magic player is attracted by Star Trek’s unique aesthetic, the most important question for Limited players is: How does the set actually play?

Polygon took part in the 24-hour early access Star Trek event on Magic Arena, and while I only had time for a dozen games between Sealed and Draft, I have one surefire takeaway: this is very different from Reality Fracture.

Limited players loved Reality Fracture for its gameplay and mechanics. Most decks fell into the midrange archetype, focusing on “value” creatures and card advantage to take over the game. The Empower Jace mechanic was the glue of the set, allowing every combination of colors to manipulate the deck through Surveil, thus helping with mana issues and granting the card draw needed to succeed in the format.

Star Trek, by contrast, feels more like The Hobbit. Based on my first impressions, the set encourages aggressive decks that want to curve out early. Every Limited environment tends to favor creatures over spells, but this seems even more true with Star Trek. Even apparently innocuous two-mana creatures like Tenacious Drone proved to be quite annoying during early access, especially when paired with the many “pump” effects available — Sarcophagus, Ship of the Dead, for example, which truly impressed me.

The Rakdos (red-black) Klingon decks seemed very solid, as they can turn up the aggression and also back it up with good removal, which is scarce in the set. Most of the removal spells cost three or more mana or are sorcery-speed. Another strong aggro deck is Gruul (red-green) Landfall, which is able to do truly disgusting things in the first turns of the game. Just look at the pictures below.

On turn 4, my opponent already had nine power on the board (potentially 10 with Planetary Patrol's Landfall effect). On turn 5, they cast a removal spell and attacked me with a total of 14 power thanks to multiple Landfall triggers. If you have a slow-to-medium start, it’s almost impossible to recover from this game state, which leads to my biggest negative impression of Star Trek: the games feel too one-sided.

All of the games I played, both in Sealed and Limited, felt very hard to turn around once one of the players got the advantage. This is typical of aggro formats that rely on curving out and quickly gaining the upper hand. Unfortunately, this can create frustration and make a Limited format grow stale quickly.

By contrast, Reality Fracture still feels fresh (and you can still play it in Arena even while Star Trek events are running) because games are more balanced and usually get decided in the last turns, based on which player has accrued more value and incremental advantage throughout the game. It’s the “classic” Magic midrange playstyle that many players still gravitate towards, even if it’s very hard to find nowadays in Constructed formats.

I drafted this Golgari (green-black) graveyard deck that felt quite strong. This is a strategy that I love to play in every format, so I was confident it could get a decent number of victories. Instead, I went 0-3. The deck was too slow and had no ways to “turn the corner” after the opponent had gained the upper hand.

Also, flooding (drawing too many lands) felt like a real issue, despite the many Surveil cards I played. I conceded a game on turn five simply because I had drawn too many lands, and my opponent was already too far ahead on the board for me to catch up. The lack of a set-wide way to mitigate bad draws is unpleasant, but I guess this is the post-Empower Jace effect. Can’t we just have that in every set?

I’m not implying that Star Trek will be an aggro-only format. Unlike The Hobbit, this is a large set, and the card pool is big enough that players can successfully build different strategies. For example, I had success with this five-color Sealed deck that simply played all the bombs, removal, fixing, and card draw I had in my pool. It was really fun. Even then, I consistently struggled to stay alive until I could deploy my bombs.

On the other hand, this simple Klingon deck also won a lot of games. It’s aggressive, has a lot of removal, and is supported by some synergies and card advantage engines to make sure you don’t run out of things to do. Red feels like a strong color in Star Trek, and it can support three of the four main aggressive archetypes.

If you’re heading to a prerelease event this weekend, my suggestion is to go back to the basics for this set. Focus on having a good curve, play a lot of creatures, and all the removal you can. Splashing is easy thanks to the many multicolored lands, but I would be wary of playing too many lands that enter tapped. As always, remember to have fun! May the Force be with you! (Did I get that right?)

#3607. ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

Among the bleakest films ever made, Werner Herzog’s “Stroszek” (1977) famously ends not with the suicide of its title character, but with a haunting coda in which a chicken pecks at a miniature piano inside a surreal roadside tourist trap’s coin-operated display. It’s a visual metaphor for the inescapable banality of life on Earth, and for the dehumanizing work people are forced to do to disguise the many failures of the American Dream. It’s also the last thing that Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis saw before he killed himself. “Look into the eyes of a chicken,” Herzog has said, “and you will see real stupidity. It is a kind of bottomless stupidity, a fiending stupidity. They are the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world.” Related Stories Inside ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’: How an R Rating, Filming in IMAX, and Epic Kaiju Battles Broke Franchise Tradition Rosamund Pike Starring in Body Horror Film ‘Feed’ for ‘Star Wars: The Acolyte’ Creator Leslye Headland

That sentiment has long endured as modern cinema’s definitive stance on chickens (despite Aardman’s best efforts), but now, after witnessing the 50 years of entropy that followed “Stroszek,” Hungarian filmmaker György Pálfi is crying fowl. Chickens are not the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world, he contends. We are. How can you tell? Easy: Just look at us through the eyes of a chicken.

A cute, cockeyed yarn that unspools like a feathered cross between “EO” and “Flow,” Pálfi’s “Hen” tells the story of a jet-black Leghorn chicken who escapes a Greek factory farm after she’s plucked from the rest of her flock because of the color of her plumage. A worker decides to take the bird home so that his wife can serve it for dinner, but our sly heroine — played by a brave hen named Feri, in addition to her seven indistinguishable stunt doubles — makes a daring escape when her captor stops his truck to refuel. But she’s snapped up again by the teeth of a dog named Titan, who carries the chicken back to the ramshackle seaside restaurant where his owner (Yannis Kokiasmenos) has much bigger problems than what to serve for dinner.

If the precise contours of those problems are a bit difficult to deduce, that’s probably because — as we’ve already established — this movie is told through the eyes of a chicken. Sometimes literally, thanks to Pálfi’s judicious deployment of POV, which is useful for times when our ruffled protagonist is, say, trapped inside a cardboard box (there’s an excellent bit where the hen starts moving the cardboard box from the inside, a “Metal Gear Solid”-inspired visual gag that proves typical of the director’s wry humor). And what does a chicken know of Europe’s ongoing migrant crisis? Of a protest between angry citizens and riot police? Of human trafficking, and the complications thereof? To judge by the film’s regular assortment of amusingly blank reaction shots, I’d wager “very little.” The titular hen doesn’t even think to look both ways when she crosses the road after flying the coop, let alone have a good answer as to why she’s doing it.

For the most part, the hen is focused on clucking her neck, surviving the pecking order at the restaurant farm where she winds up, and potentially even laying a few eggs of her own someday (we see her hatch in the movie’s first scene, but they grow up so fast). Most of the human drama is relegated to the distant background, as Pálfi mines the humor from his movie’s conceit by using the restaurant as a lens onto the hen’s predicament rather than the other way around. The people are mere archetypes, but some of the animals we meet appear so layered and inscrutable that you’d happily watch a three-hour Nathan Fielder documentary about them. (The terse and fiery courtship between the star hen and her most aggressive suitor is soundtracked by a classic Greek love song, a flourish that stands out in a film where desperate migrants are being left for dead just off-camera.)

Then again, couldn’t every film about — and starring — real live animals be considered a documentary to some extent? Feri the chicken has been trained by the best of the business, but she remains blissfully unaware of the camera, and Pálfi takes pains not to anthropomorphize her any more than necessary. Plenty of heightened enjoyment comes elsewhere, much of it laundered through Giorgos Karvelas’ saturated cinematography, Szabolcs Szoke’s hyper-dynamic score, and the furtive way Pálfi bends the film’s crafts into something that almost resembles a chicken’s idea of a Western.

Here, the hen is a hen is a hen, and while “Hen” is prone to long and repetitive stretches in which she basically just hens around as a result of that approach, the animal’s natural obliviousness is too crucial a contrast to our own willful antipathy for Pálfi to risk muddying the difference between the two. At the risk of making the movie’s side-eyed social commentary sound more didactic than it is in practice (save for one very pointed moment towards the end that explicitly affirms Herzog’s claim), “Hen” uses a chicken’s lack of moral responsibility to highlight the mandate we have to heed our own, no matter how effectively we’ve evolved to ignore it.

No matter how good we get at farming other species, and killing our own. Pálfi does very little to goose or otherwise manipulate our emotional attachment to his chicken star, but there’s still something to be said for how easily we become more invested in this witless hen’s fate than in that of the doomed people with whom she crosses paths. By the time it reaches its end, this strange but sober film starts to point back to the beginning, cutting from a single egg being squeezed out of a hen’s vent (Google says “vent”) to a vast sea of them bobbling around inside the factory’s machines. One is easy to follow, and to care about. Thousands are a statistic. We’re smart enough to farm other animals, but people — like chickens — won’t hesitate to eat each other the minute they get hungry.

Dekanalog will release “Hen” in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3606. The Walking Dead Officially Reunites Glenn And Maggie In Aftermath

Glenn and Maggie managed to find love and keep their romance alive through a literal apocalypse, cementing their relationship as an all-time fan favorite in The Walking Dead canon. From their first encounters at Hershel's farm in Season 2, Steven Yeun and Lauren Cohan brought a much-needed warmth to a series steeped in relentless brutality and death.

As The Walking Dead became one of television's biggest shows, their relationship remained an emotional anchor, surviving through devastating loss over the years. Eventually marrying and preparing to start a family, Glenn and Maggie offered proof that a future was still possible, even after civilization had collapsed.

Unfortunately, that hope was shattered by Glenn's infamous death in Season 7, which aired ten years ago now, in a moment that permanently changed Maggie's future and the franchise itself. Cohan eventually returned to lead the spinoff The Walking Dead: Dead City, but sadly, Glenn's fate was sealed forever. Now, a decade after his heartbreaking farewell, the beloved character is officially reuniting with Maggie in a surprising new franchise release.

Glenn and Maggie are officially back together in The Walking Dead: Aftermath, giving fans an unexpected reunion nearly a decade after Glenn's devastating death in the original series. The officially licensed game, developed by Swift Games and published by Ares Interactive in partnership with AMC, brings both characters back as playable survivors alongside other familiar faces from the franchise.

Originally released in July, Aftermath has gradually expanded its roster over the past few months, with Maggie and Glenn joining the action through subsequent updates. Their return doesn't undo Glenn's death or establish a new storyline for the couple, but it does allow players to recruit both characters and bring them back into the same group of survivors—arguably the closest thing we'll ever get to a proper reunion.

Better still, Glenn and Maggie have their own distinct weapons, abilities, and combat styles. Glenn is classified as an "Epic Acid" survivor specializing in shotguns, wielding a tactical shotgun and throwing knives to take out enemies. He focuses on attack speed, positioning, and Acid damage, obviously.

Maggie, meanwhile, is an "Epic Fire" survivor who specializes in blades, mines, and burning enemies. Her signature Burning Land ability creates an expanding ring of fire that damages nearby walkers, giving her a completely different approach to combat.

As for the game itself, Aftermath is a free-to-play roguelite survival action game, with intense battles against dangerous walker hordes, and with camp management and character progression as well. Players can also recruit characters like Rick Grimes, Daryl Dixon, and Michonne, upgrade equipment, gather resources, and strengthen their settlements. Regular updates have introduced a ton of new content since launch, including a competitive Rivals mode.

So far, The Walking Dead: Aftermath has been a relatively big success among players. As of early November, the game has a 4.6/5 rating on Google Play, with roughly 50,000 reviews and more than a million downloads, while the App Store has it listed with a 4.8/5 rating from roughly 5k ratings. Fans can download and play Aftermath on Android smartphones and tablets, iPhone, and iPad, while Google Play also lists Windows PC availability. Noteably, both mobile versions feature optional in-app purchases, but the game is technically free.

#3605. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3604. The 8 Greatest Crime Thriller Opening Scenes, Ranked

You only get one chance to make a good first impression, and it's particularly true in crime thriller cinema. The opening scene of any film allows it to establish the stakes, story, and setting, but it is also an opportunity to completely shatter or solidify audience expectations. This has been done in many different ways throughout the near-100-year history of crime cinema, taking the form of anything from action-packed crime scenes and high-octane police chases to meditative descents into a detective’s or a criminal’s psyche.

But it is little surprise that the very best opening scenes in crime thriller movies have been the ones that dared to do things a little differently, be it a juxtaposition in tone and text, an uncommonly brilliant piece of technical filmmaking, or even a simple conversation. Ranging from the dread-inducing openings of classical film noir to viscerally intense starts to modern masterpieces, these crime thrillers deliver some of the best first scenes ever shot.

It may be more of a sequence than one set scene, but Drive’s opening is a compelling mixture of tension and style that immediately hooks viewers. It opens with Ryan Gosling’s unnamed Driver stating his terms on the phone, the camera slowly panning across his dimly lit apartment. He picks up the getaway vehicle, then drives to the scene of a robbery to pick up the two thieves, navigate the police response, and drop them off safely and undetected.

Director Nicholas Winding Refn masterfully builds suspense through patience, precise sound design, and concentrated cinematography, with the camera’s perspective never leaving the inside of the car from the moment the heist begins. Drive immediately breaks away from action norms by avoiding bombastic, full-throttle carnage, instead extracting a sense of simmering suspense through The Driver’s clinical, chess-like strategy that favors stealth over speed. Basking in the gorgeous, noir-inspired visuals that define the movie’s aesthetic, Drive’s opening is a masterclass in technical filmmaking and stylistic storytelling.

1958’s Vertigo is one of the defining thrillers in Hollywood cinema, a gripping tale of obsession, desire, and mystique realized with some of the most innovative and impactful filmmaking of its era. It establishes its excellence from the opening scene, which sees San Francisco detective John “Scottie” Ferguson (James Stewart) and a uniform cop chase a criminal across rooftops. When Ferguson slips on a steep rooftop, his colleague attempts to help him, only to fall to his death.

It is an astonishing introduction to Ferguson’s trauma, which leads to him developing a debilitating fear of heights and retiring from the force to work as a private eye. However, it is also an unrelenting masterpiece of technical filmmaking. Perhaps its most notable achievement is its invention of the dolly-zoom, which brings a sense of disorienting terror to Ferguson’s POV shot as he looks down at the ground. Also bolstered by Bernard Herrmann’s swirling, spiraling score, Vertigo’s opening scene is a triumph of cinematic tension that then bleeds into what is one of the greatest opening credit sequences of all time.

In some ways, No Country for Old Men begins exactly how you’d expect from a neo-Western crime thriller: gorgeous shots of the American landscape, a growing sense of tension, Sheriff Bell’s (Tommy Lee Jones) poignant narration. In many ways, though, the movie is completely subversive. It refuses to offer exposition or explanation; it even refuses to use a score, instead opting to emphasize the sparse ambience of the desert, with gentle winds and the crunch of gravel under two men's feet being all that breaks the silence.

This approach highlights the movie’s bleak tone and hostile setting. The Coen Brothers evoke suspense through a sense of numbness that is overlaid by Bell’s poetic meditation on how the nature of crime has changed. Cutting to a police station where arrested criminal Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) ruthlessly kills the cop who apprehended him, No Country for Old Men launches into its unflinching descent into violence, morality, fate, and changing times with astonishing conviction, making for one of the most compelling opening passages crime cinema has ever seen.

The annals of crime thriller cinema are filled with iconic, terrifying scenes that set the audience on edge and conjure a sense of sickening tension. Few, however, can rival the piercing impact of Sicario’s first sequence. Plunging viewers into the brutal, unglamorous reality of cartel violence, it presents an FBI raid on a safe house in Arizona with the objective of rescuing hostages. After a rogue shot from a thug’s shotgun, the agents discover the newly plastered walls of the house are filled with corpses.

It is a sequence of faultless suspense, with the deep, dull drum beat and ominous string crescendos of Jóhann Jóhannsson's score instilling cold dread in viewers. Roger Deakins’ clinical, concise cinematography and the use of protagonist Kate Macer (Emily Blunt) as an audience surrogate further increase the tension. We share Kate's confusion, shock, and mounting horror as she is confronted with a world of evil and violence she can’t initially understand. Ending with a frightful explosion as agents realize the house is booby-trapped, Denis Villeneuve opens Sicario with a sequence of stomach-churning intensity.

Insurance salesman Walter Neff (Fred MacMurray) staggers into his office in the middle of the night, removes his coat to display a gunshot wound, lights a cigarette one-handed, then starts recording a confession of a fraudulent claim scheme he himself was involved in. He confesses to murder, to conspiracy, and he even confesses: “I killed him for money and a woman. I didn’t get the money, and I didn’t get the woman.”

Film noir is no stranger to fatalistic doom—the idea is basically the thematic backbone of the genre—but few movies capture it with the same immediacy and impact as Double Indemnity. Framing the deadly con as Neff’s confession after the fact imbues this classic with a resigned sense of damnation. Audiences know Neff’s ploy is going to go bad, but how and when becomes the tantalizing question. Only compounded by Billy Wilder’s impeccable use of high-contrast lighting and deft shot selection, as well as the dry, cynical wit of his and Raymond Chandler’s dialogue, Double Indemnity is the epitome of hard-boiled noir tragedy.

Few filmmakers are as proficient at engrossing audiences as Quentin Tarantino. From the unrelenting suspense of Inglourious Basterds to the playful ‘60s Western TV promo in Once Upon a Time in... Hollywood, his movies make an instant impression, but few do it quite like Pulp Fiction. The 1994 crime classic begins with a couple conversing over breakfast about the growing risks they face making a living as armed robbers before deciding to switch to holding up restaurants, starting with that very diner.

A sweet, romantic kiss cascades into an eruption of violence and profanity, then Dick Dale’s “Misirlou” ushers in the opening credits. Viewers are instantly engrossed, with Tarantino’s trademark dialogue and the magnetic performances of Tim Roth and Amanda Plummer working in tandem to conjure one of the most hypnotic and energizing opening scenes of all time. That the movie returns to and recontextualizes the sequence in its final scene only makes it even better.

Children play in the street while a mother readies the table for supper, a young girl bounces her ball against a wall, and then the shadow of a man nears her, covering the poster declaring a reward for anyone who has information that brings an at-large child killer to justice. The man—who we soon learn is Hans Beckert (Peter Lorre)—walks with the child and buys her a balloon. It cuts to the mother, who speaks briefly with a visitor before calling her daughter in for dinner, but her calls go unanswered.

The way Fritz Lang starts M doesn’t feature any violence, conflict, or visual displays of criminal wrongdoing, and yet it's one of the most haunting opening sequences in cinematic history. Beckert’s predatory evil is presented through what isn’t shown, while the way it plays out so invisibly and quickly is truly chilling. M marked Lang’s first departure from silent cinema, but the strength of visual storytelling silent movies demand is on full display in a magnetically eerie opening scene to what remains one of the genre’s greatest ever movies.

Crime thriller cinema is littered with outstanding opening scenes, but in terms of craft, tension, and impact, it is impossible to look beyond 1958’s Touch of Evil as being a definitive standout. Directed by Orson Welles, the gritty film noir classic opens with a three-and-a-half-minute long shot that sees a time bomb planted in the boot of a car before the owners return to their vehicle and start driving through the busy streets of the U.S.-Mexico border town.

The one-take approach works on so many levels. It introduces viewers to the nightlife and style of the setting, immerses them in a frenetic soundscape that shifts seamlessly between conversations and car radios, and evokes an unbearable sense of suspense, accentuating the ticking clock on the inevitable explosion. It is most engrossing as an incredible feat of large-scale choreography and precise camerawork, but Touch of Evil’s opening sequence also establishes the film’s sense of moral decay and cultural friction. It is high stakes, style, and storytelling done to perfection, and it marks one of the most arresting and awe-inspiring openings to any movie ever made.
