#3603. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3602. ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups

There are dozens of scenes that capture “North of North’s” digestible, defiant kindness, but my favorite arrives near the start of the second season’s second episode. Siaja (Anna Lambe) wakes up, grabs a glass of water, and promptly spits it out. The local water supply is contaminated (“They must’ve cranked those chemicals again,” her mom says), so Siaja heads to the nearest store to load up on jugs of clean water. Outside, there’s an elderly woman perched on her snowmobile, smoking a cigarette, who loudly hassles Siaja for a little charity.

“Must be nice,” the woman shouts, getting Siaja’s attention. “[You] buying filtered water. It’s too expensive [for me]. [I] gotta drink government pool water. Back in the day, we had nice ice straight from the river. Pure, nice, and healthy.” Related Stories ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

On that last word, “healthy,” the woman takes a drag from her cigarette, and while she’s doubled over coughing, Siaja takes her forceful hint and puts one of her water jugs in the woman’s cart. “Here, you take this,” Siaja says. The woman, speaking in Inuktitut, does not say “thank you”; she asks if she can keep the jug. Then she hacks a loogie into the snow as Siaja drives off, punctuating just how little the gesture means to her.

Now, it’s clear this woman knows exactly what she’s doing. She didn’t end up outside the town’s only source for clean water by accident, and Siaja knows it. But she also knows the woman is telling the truth: She’s too old to get ice for herself, and she’s too poor to afford purified water. Siaja also knows this woman is her elder, and elders should be taken care of. So after acquiescing in the moment, Siaja expands on the idea soon after: She grabs Alistair (Jay Ryan), her big, burly dad, and they go get blocks of ice from the river to deliver around town — for free.

Of course, it doesn’t go exactly as planned (the rivers aren’t all “pure” and “healthy” anymore), but Siaja’s chance encounter with the woman serves as the impetus for the entire episode: Siaja uses it to prove to her boss that she can be more than an assistant at the community center. She bonds with her dad, who she’s still getting to know. She sets a good example for her daughter, Bun (Keira Belle Cooper), and she still finds time to flirt with her crush, Kuuk (Braeden Clarke), in between deliveries.

Siaja is doing exactly what she set out to do from the start of the season: “level up” her life.

Reading it back now, the story sounds corny. But despite all that positive energy driving so many warm-hearted gestures, “North by North” never becomes saccharine. Siaja’s triumphs don’t feel like cheap schmaltz. They hit that tricky TV sweet spot, where characters’ helpful actions and benevolent intentions feel genuine even when, on paper, they seem too nice to be tolerable.

It helps, of course, that Siaja fucks up early and often. Nothing makes a win land like taking many embarrassing losses to get there, as she did in Season 1 after summoning the courage to leave her husband, get a job, and start fresh — with an adorable daughter in tow. In Season 2, her plan to charm tourists doesn’t go over as whimsically as she imagined. Her plan to get her own place doesn’t include dropping in the rankings on an endless waiting list for affordable housing. Her plan to ditch her small-minded ex-husband (who doesn’t appear in Season 2) doesn’t include sitting for rounds of speed-dating or waiting out a relationship that may never end.

Siaja’s self-actualization isn’t as easy as ditching the zero to get with the hero, even when she’s her own hero from the jump — it takes time to learn the ins and outs of public service, to connect with people, and to make sense of your own emotions. “North of North” respects each process while savoring her struggle through them. (Lambe’s comic timing remains pitch-perfect, and her ability to navigate tonal swings is just as sharp.)

Investing in Siaja’s incremental progress does wonders to keep “North of North” from feeling like forgettable fluff — especially when the back-half of Season 2 gets heavy wrestling with familial, cultural, and communal responsibilities — but none of it work without the attention to detail surrounding Siaja, too. When the first season premiered in January 2025, “North by North” earned plenty of well-deserved praise for its authenticity. The fictional town of Ice Cove represents real communities in Nunavet, the northernmost part of Canada within the Arctic Circle, and the series employed a heavily Indigenous cast and crew to help bring it to life.

And what life there is: Season 2 is rich with cultural specifics, from a Greenlandic mask-dancing celebration to public safety concerns. (Beyond the bad water, don’t forget to place your beer orders early! A birthday without a brewski could be your last!) Every episode whisks you away to a very cold, very kind small town, which is oh-so-welcoming on chilly winter evenings when you just want to bask in the season’s cozy glow.

Respecting and highlighting Inuk customs is step one. Step two expands the idea by grounding “North by North” in perspectives beyond their beloved lead screwup. That way, her work ethic and generosity stay sweet and meaningful (when overexposure could easily turn them sour) and the show’s overall tone avoids becoming rote. Siaja’s mom, Neevee (Maika Harper), is the sardonic balance her daughter demands, and how they flesh out her backstory to explain her sharp disposition offers some of the season’s strongest scenes. Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub), Siaja’s boss, is an oblivious white lady desperate to be cherished as a leader, and her pushy ambitions help clarify Siaja’s unselfish aid to others (while generating laughs).

And then there’s the townsfolk, who may not always be as colorful as the woman demanding free water, but who share her fair yet formidable spirit. If Siaja’s community service was met with cheers and applause, it would be unbelievable. That’s not how citizens treat their local officials. But their measured disposition isn’t just authentic, it’s essential. Similarly, if the citizens were the butt of every joke (like in “Parks and Recreation”), Siaja’s dedication could feel misplaced. If they were mean, like too many real-life city council visitors, her above-and-beyond gestures could seem foolish. Instead, Siaja’s community is just there, living their own lives, waiting for her to get her shit together and do what’s right by them.

“North of North” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 5 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3601. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3600. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3599. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Players Need To Change This Setting Before Doing Anything Else

Fiddling around in a settings menu isn't necessarily what comes to mind first when thinking about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but when it comes to the remake, long-time Nintendo fans might benefit from giving it a go. While there's no need to mess with much — and it's not a game that offers an endless array of tweaks regardless — one basic toggle could have a huge impact on the overall Ocarina of Time experience.

Perhaps the most fundamental change in the Ocarina of Time remake is the introduction of a jump button, which changes the very nature of Link's traversal throughout Hyrule and all the dungeons it holds. The first 3D Zelda game to fully embrace jumping was Breath of the Wild, and in Ocarina of Time's default settings, it carries over Breath of the Wild's controversial default control choice.

Unlike most games, Breath of the Wild, Tears of the Kingdom, and the Ocarina of Time remake all assign the jump button to X by default. This makes sense on an abstract level, associating upward movement with the face button that sits above the rest on a Switch or Switch 2 controller. For many players, however, it works against years of muscle memory, as jumping is usually assigned to the A or B button in games like the Super Mario series.

Recalibrating isn't that big of a deal, but for those who find the change fundamentally alienating (like Reddit user clarence87boddicker), it's easy to take care of. The Options menu in the Ocarina of Time remake features a toggle to change the binding to B, restoring a more traditional control scheme.

For those who already adjusted to jumping with X in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, this might not be a big deal, and doing so could actually feel more comfortable overall. Not every Zelda fan has played them, though, and even some who did play them made the same choice to rebind the jump button. It's also easy to fall out of the habit after playing the games, as other titles can quickly reactivate the B button muscle memory.

At any rate, Nintendo's clearly all-in on the X to jump initiative, as Donkey Kong Bananza adopted the same concept. Despite sharing a lot of DNA with Super Mario Odyssey, which stuck to a traditional scheme, it leaned even further into the directional nature of the face buttons, associating B with downward movement instead. In games where this isn't as relevant, Nintendo hasn't yet made the switch to jumping with X, and the Mario games still haven't made such radical changes.

Regardless of where you stand in the debate, it's best to take stock of the options and choose your preference before starting Link's grand journey. Few things take away from the sense of adventure like a disconnect with the controls that guide it, so those who already know they prefer to jump with B — and are confident that their preferences won't change — should make sure to switch things up at the start of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

#3598. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3597. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026 during the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Another melancholically splenetic Martin McDonagh jag about a banter-mad pair of murderers who go on a boys trip to purgatory (where they search their souls as they wait for death to find them), the prickly but unconvincing “Wild Horse Nine” strains to translate the post-Guy Ritchie bark of “In Bruges” into the language of a classic American Western. In this case, an American Western set on Easter Island and backdropped by Augusto Pinochet’s rise to power in the fall of 1973.  Related Stories ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

McDonagh’s decision to recast his same old script against the backdrop of such a real and terrible event grants this new telling a welcome sense of scale, both in terms of its characters’ morality, as well as in regards to their greater place in history. But that decision is a double-edged sword that cuts the film off at the knees. Where “In Bruges” kicked off with the killing of a fictional altar boy, “Wild Horse Nine” is overshadowed by the deaths of thousands upon thousands of very real people, and that reality bleeds into the edges of the frame even when the seriocomic absurdity of McDonagh’s writing demands a world of pure invention.

Does the overlap make “Wild Horse Nine” feel glib? Yes, and thank god for that — if not for glibness the movie would lose the majority of its few solid laughs. The problem is that it also makes “Wild Horse Nine” feel as transparently manufactured as the CIA-backed overthrow of a foreign democracy. I can accept that an inexperienced hitman might have a dark night of the soul after shooting an innocent child during confession. By contrast, I struggle to believe that a veteran CIA agent who openly brags about his involvement in the Kennedy assassination would have a come-to-Jesus moment after orchestrating the demise of Salvador Allende. McDonagh has some good fun wrestling with whether or not we should care about such a mottled change of heart, but the point is gradually rendered moot in a movie whose emotions are less credible than its conspiracies.

The original Company man, Chris (John Malkovich, more locked in than he’s been on screen since “Burn After Reading”) is a natural hinge for the off-kilter comedy that McDonagh builds around him, in that he can be a joy to watch even when you don’t buy a word he’s saying. More than just an ordinary CIA agent, he’s the living personification of America’s efforts to destabilize foreign governments across the 20th century. He was close with Patrice Lumumba until the day the Congolese leader was executed by a firing squad. He was in Cuba to spur on the exiles who failed to overthrow Fidel Castro in 1961. He was even in Dallas, USA on a Friday afternoon in November 1963, doing things his ornery boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) would much prefer he didn’t tell you about.

He traveled to all of those places, and got all of those people killed, with the blithe imperiousness of a flag waving in the wind. Chris says that he’s killed 68 people over the course of his career, and he offers that information as easily as a rumor — in a way that makes it sound like the number could be half that, or double, and it wouldn’t make a difference.

Recently, fate has blown Chris and his office husband/platonic life partner/exasperated straightman Lee (McDonagh vet Sam Rockwell) down south to Chile, where the two of them have been hard at work orchestrating the September 11th coup against the democratically elected socialist president, knowing full well that it would plunge the country into decades of brutal dictatorship. Chris appears to delight in sowing chaos, and the fact that he gets to wear a cute little Panama hat while he does it only boosts his joie de vivre.

But Chris is fraying at the seams in ways that we can’t see at first — ways that will only begin to reveal themselves when he and Lee decide to celebrate their imminent success with a sightseeing trip to Easter Island, a short 2,300 miles off the Western coast of Santiago. There are still a couple of months to go before the coup, but the wheels are in motion, and there’s little for these men to do for now besides fly to Rapa Nui, look at the “big heads,” flirt with a couple of beautiful young leftists (the prissier but gentler of whom is played by “Ema” mega-talent Mariana di Girolamo), and mordantly reflect upon their role in the awfulness Pinochet will soon inflict upon his own people. That task is complicated and confused by the fact that Chris seems to be losing his memory, which casts Lee in the role of his peevish but loving caretaker.

“Wild Horse Nine” is only the second feature that’s ever been shot on the ultra-remote soil of Rapa Nui (Kevin Reynolds’ 1994 epic “Rapa Nui” is credited as the first), and McDonagh rightly exalts in the fact that he’s brought Hollywood to the end of the world. The first half of his movie largely adheres to the fiction that Chris and Lee are just on Easter Island to fuck around, which offers a semi-relaxed opportunity for us to take in the sights. Ben Davis’ sun-bleached cinematography renders the hills and beaches of Rapa Nui with the veneer of a lost idyll, the ancient moai statues assuming an especially sacred charge when contrasted against such profane characters.

Chris bemusedly laughs the statues off with ethnographic glee, mocking one of the shorter figures as a dwarf (in case the “In Bruges” déjà vu wasn’t already strong enough), but it’s clear that he’s shaken by the fact that some of them almost 750 years old. That they’ve stood there in silent tribute to Polynesia’s ancestors as empires rose and fell on faraway shores, each of them a graveyard of forgotten people just like him. By the same token, it’s similarly clear that he’s trying to get at something in his own mind as he and Lee listen to Judy Collins in their rental car, argue over whether or not any Nazis made it into heaven (among other even more aggressively screen-written subjects), and whisper sweet nothings to the wild horses that run about the island, but the specific nature of that something is hard for him to pin down.

Malkovich has the time of his life with that search for Chris’ last speck of humanity, which shines up from the bottom of his soul as his mind continues to erode. At once both insidiously relaxed and also choked with Catholic guilt, Malkovich’s performance marries the nonchalance of a cowboy to the paranoia of a bounty target. One minute he’s waxing poetic about dinosaurs, and the next he’s rigging his luggage with explosives (maybe) and checking the “Memento”-like reminder notes he’s slipped into his jacket pocket.

“Wild Horse Nine” loves Chris too much to pretend like we’re not supposed to, but Malkovich never asks for our sympathy because he knows that he’ll get it anyway, and not just because the purpose of Rockwell’s character is to ensure that we do. It’s Chris’ job to make rooting for the bad guys feel like the right choice. It’s the cornerstone of America’s post-war foreign policy.

So while Chris might be cut from the same cloth as John Wayne (to the extent that Monument Valley is revealed to be a place of great importance to him), his arc is aimed in the opposite direction of the one that Ethan Edwards traces across “The Searchers”; Chris is a major asshole this movie gradually puckers into a wayward hero, and while it’s all too easy to root for him to complete that transformation before time runs out, at no point does “Wild Horse Nine” sell us on the premise that it would mean anything in the end — even to him.

The movie, blessedly, isn’t Catholic enough to offer Chris a big moment of divine expiation; in lieu of building to a grand confession, he and Lee simply run afoul of their CIA higher-ups until their PTO turns into a matter of American national security. Guns are fired. Hostages are taken. The word “fuck” is used like a punctuation mark, and regrets are muttered into the wind long after there’s any way for them to matter.

It all gets a bit too busy and madcap as “Wild Horse Nine” — freighted with sadness during even its cheekiest bits, as is McDonagh’s way — scrambles to make up for the general listlessness of its first half. Never as funny as it is sardonic, and always reaching so hard to be more of both, the film’s most successful moments are mined from the ambient tension between memory and erasure.

Chris, we begin to suspect, would do anything to forget what he’s done, and his own mind is graciously willing to get him halfway there. The rest of the CIA will do anything it takes to make sure that Chris doesn’t share whatever it is that he still remembers. Surrounding them on all sides are statues that predated America by several hundred years, and will likely continue to watch over Rapa Nui long after our empire has been wiped away like a tear in the rain. In “Wild Horse Nine,” American interventionism is less effective as the set-up for some jokes than it is as their punchline.

“Wild Horse Nine” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3596. 6 Fantasy Books Better Than Harry Potter

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Harry Potter showed us how magical it feels to grow up alongside characters you love. These six books capture different parts of that experience, from discovering worlds you never knew existed to facing dangers that change who you are. And the worlds themselves are just as inviting.

There's a twelve-year-old criminal mastermind caught in a standoff with fairies, a kingdom trapped in endless winter, and a wardrobe that leads four siblings straight into its troubles. Yet beneath all that magic, the books on this list are filled with friendship, difficult choices, and characters worth caring about, and that is what made Harry Potter so memorable in the first place. Let's get started.

Artemis Fowl begins with a boy who seems impossible to root for, twelve-year-old Artemis kidnaps Holly Short, a fairy officer, and demands ransom to restore his family’s fortune. He already has a plan, a captive, and a price. Then the fairies arrive as an armed, organized, technologically advanced force, unlike the harmless folklore Artemis thinks he can outsmart.

The siege becomes a contest between Artemis’s confidence that everything can be controlled and Holly’s refusal to accept his rules. Butler’s loyalty gives Artemis’s schemes a human cost. At the same time, Holly’s courage forces him to recognize a mind he cannot simply buy. That uneasy change is the book’s real pleasure. Eoin Colfer makes intelligence exciting, then asks what it’s worth if Artemis uses it only to serve himself.

Morrigan Crow has been blamed for every misfortune around her, and she expects to die on her eleventh birthday. Then Jupiter North takes her to Nevermoor, where she must compete for a place in the Wundrous Society. The challenge is that the trials demand a special talent, and Morrigan is convinced she has none.

That makes the competition more affecting than a string of clever tests. Above all, Morrigan is testing whether Jupiter’s belief in her is real, and if the first person who ever chose her will keep choosing her. The city’s oddities and the Society’s dangerous trials bring plenty of fantasy adventure, but the question underneath them is painfully recognizable, what if everyone else has already decided what you’re worth? Jessica Townsend turns Morrigan’s search for home into the real engine of Nevermoor. It is a brilliant, unforgettable start to the series.

Percy Jackson’s voice is the first reason to read The Lightning Thief. He meets danger with suspicion, jokes, and the particular irritation of a kid who keeps being told that his life is his own fault. When Zeus’s master lightning bolt is stolen and Percy becomes the prime suspect, he travels across the country with Grover and Annabeth to return it before the gods’ conflict becomes a war.

With Rick Riordan at the helm, Greek mythology becomes Percy's immediate reality, where classroom myths suddenly become the rules for surviving monsters, gods, and betrayal. Percy’s friendship with Annabeth grows through shared danger. Then, Luke’s choice gives the ending a sting that lasts beyond the quest. The book is funny, but the jokes never make Percy’s fear or loyalty feel trivial. It’s fast, witty, and every bit as addictive as a trip to King's Cross.

Lyra Belacqua lives among the scholars of Jordan College with Pantalaimon, her dæmon, who can change shape. When children begin disappearing, including Lyra’s friend Roger, she follows their trail north. At Bolvangar, she finds the Gobblers’ terrible work as they cut children away from their dæmons. Philip Pullman makes that horror personal by giving the missing children names, friendships, and futures Lyra wants to protect.

Lyra is brave, but she is still a child making choices with incomplete knowledge. That matters most at the end, when Lord Asriel uses Roger’s death to open a passage between worlds. Lyra follows him through it with Pan. It doesn't let you rest easy for a second, abruptly stealing away the comfort of a clean rescue. Pullman gives the reader a victory, a profound loss, and a reason to follow Lyra into the next book.

In Ursula K. Le Guin’s A Wizard of Earthsea, Ged’s trouble starts because he wants to prove how powerful he is. At the school of wizardry on Roke, he attempts a forbidden spell and brings a shadow-creature into the world. From then on, his education has less to do with winning approval and more to do with accepting responsibility for what he has done.

The book gives its magic rules real moral weight, proving that names matter, power has limits, and trying to dominate what you fear only makes matters worse. Ged spends much of the book fleeing the creature he unleashed. At last, he turns to face it and speaks its name, which happens to be his own. The resolution is startlingly simple and deeply earned. Instead of relying on brute strength, Ged overcomes the shadow by finally understanding what he has been running from and accepting it as part of himself. That is a wizard’s story with real wisdom in it.

In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, Lucy steps through a wardrobe and finds Narnia under the White Witch’s rule, frozen in winter. Edmund’s meeting with the Witch makes the danger personal when he wants her approval and the Turkish delight she offers, betraying his siblings to get both. The novel lets that choice stay ugly. Edmund acts out of genuine selfishness, putting the people he loves at risk.

Then Aslan offers himself in Edmund’s place. The Stone Table, the Witch’s bargain, and Aslan’s return give the book its strongest claim, proving that guilt can be real without making a person impossible to forgive. That moral weight sits beside the pleasure of Lucy meeting Mr. Tumnus, the siblings traveling together, and Narnia changing as the Witch loses control. The story stays remarkably clear throughout. C.S. Lewis made it simple enough to read as a child while still giving an adult plenty to feel.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

#3595. ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

Yellow Veil Pictures has boarded North American distribution rights for Callum Devlin‘s “The Weed Eaters,” a New Zealand cannibal horror film that notched a best feature win at SXSW Sydney in 2025. The indie banner is planning a winter release.

The deal for “The Weed Eaters” comes after the independent feature first debuted in the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store, a video-on-demand streaming platform launched by the film-focused social media platform in 2025.

“Yellow Veil are consistently putting out the richest cinematic meals on offer, so it’s a real honour for ‘The Weed Eaters’ to be a part of their roster,” director Devlin wrote in a statement included in the deal’s announcement. “We always knew there was a global audience for this movie. I mean, this film is pretty gross. But the people that are into it are super into it, and we’re more than happy to make movies for the stoner freaks of the world.” Related Stories Inside Letterboxd’s Unlikely Distribution Pipeline: How ‘It Ends’ and Other Gems Found Their Way to a Deal Letterboxd Sale Talks Are Heating Up

“‘The Weed Eaters’ exemplifies what we have come to expect from New Zealand indie films. It’s filled with heart and humor, but this one’s not afraid to get weird and gross along the way,” reads a statement from Yellow Veil.

Exact details on the release plan for “The Weed Eaters” went undisclosed, though Yellow Veil is primarily a digital distribution company with ventures into limited theatrical play.

“The Weed Eaters” follows four friends that have their holiday getaway upended when they stumble upon a strain of marijuana that makes tokers crave the taste of human flesh. The film comes from Sports Team, Horse Bite, and Causeway Films, the Australian banner that was also behind titles like “The Babadook,” “Leviticus,” and “Bring Her Back.”

Prior to “The Weed Eaters,” several other titles featured on the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store have gone on to land wider distribution, with one of the best-known examples being Neon’s acquisition of the cerebral horror film “It Ends.”

“We would never presume whether these filmmakers want to have a traditional distribution,” Letterboxd’s head of Video Store content Courtney Mayhew told IndieWire in August. “Even if it’s just five really strong ambassadors for these independent gems who will sing their praises and push for it and tell their friends about it … that’s something that has value.”

#3594. Brandon Sanderson's Stormlight: Herald Officially Releases November 2027

Fans have been waiting patiently for the return of Brandon Sanderson's The Stormlight Archive, but the wait for the next chapter of Roshar's story is finally starting to inch its way closer. Following the release of Wind and Truth in 2024, Sanderson stepped away from the series to focus on other Cosmere projects, leaving readers wondering when the promised "Back Five" would finally begin to take shape.

Fortunately, his latest update offered some encouraging news. Sanderson has already begun the early outlining process for the second half of the saga, with plans to spend 2027 mapping out Books 6 through 10 before beginning to write the sixth installment in January 2028. The next novel is still years away, but at least the road back to Roshar is on the map.

In the meantime, The Stormlight Archive has been quite busy elsewhere. The extraordinary success of Stormlight: War for Roshar has shown just how enthusiastic the fanbase remains, and the official confirmation of Stormlight: Herald offers yet another exciting development for fans eager to see the franchise expand.

Brotherwise Games has officially confirmed Herald as part of its enormously successful Stormlight: War for Roshar Kickstarter campaign, which concluded on November 5, with more than $3.6 million pledged by nearly 15,000 backers. While Herald isn't a separate game, it's the campaign's highest pledge tier, offering an enormous collection of Stormlight Archive and Cosmere tabletop releases for fans who supported the project at the $375 level.

The Herald pledge includes everything offered in the $295 Fifth Ideal tier, beginning with the upcoming War for Roshar strategy board game and its Champions Expansion. Backers will also receive a collection of deluxe upgrades, including enhanced 3D components, custom card sleeves, premium wooden army tokens, and the applicable stretch-goal rewards unlocked during the campaign.

Beyond the main game, Herald includes four additional Cosmere miniature releases:

These miniature collections expand the range of characters and creatures available to fans, with figures suitable for display or use in the larger Cosmere Roleplaying Game. The Kickstarter also offered other optional add-ons, including the earlier Stormlight 2024 miniature collection, the Gargantuan Chasmfiend, and miniature bundles inspired by the previous Stormlight Archive novels.

Perhaps the biggest incentive for choosing Herald, though, was the inclusion of three additional Cosmere tabletop releases beyond War for Roshar itself. Backers who selected the tier will also receive Mistborn: The Deckbuilding Game, the Well of Ascension expansion, and Shards of Creation.

All of these goodies made Herald a very appealing package for longtime Sanderson fans, bringing together multiple games inspired by his interconnected fantasy universe. While Mistborn: The Deckbuilding Game is a card-driven experience inspired by Scadrial's magical abilities, Shards of Creation explores the broader Cosmere through a separate competitive card game.

As for War for Roshar itself, the upcoming strategy game will allow players to command forces representing Honor and Odium, recruiting iconic characters, developing armies, and using Surgebinding abilities as they compete for control of Roshar.

Brotherwise Games currently expects War for Roshar to begin fulfilling Kickstarter orders in November 2027, with a broader retail release planned around the 2027 holiday season. All items included in the Herald pledge are expected to ship together, including the previously released Cosmere games, meaning backers should anticipate receiving their complete bundles toward the end of next year.

#3593. ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

Regional film festivals matter to a movie’s more cosmic position in the awards season, even if it started somewhere like Venice, Toronto, Telluride, Cannes, or even Sundance. They generate excitement from real-world audiences (and often Oscar voters, as in Middleburg, Virginia), and they also help unspool headlines that keep films top of mind for those who follow the race.

The 49th Denver Film Festival, held in the hip, high-altitude Colorado city every year, just wrapped its annual event — which this year ran October 22 to November 1. Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith, artistic director Matthew Campbell, and their team brought out special guests including Carrie Coon, John Leguizamo, John Cho, D’Arcy Carden, Peter Gamble, Indya Moore, Hans Petter Moland, and more to receive prizes and be feted with special tributes. Several of these, including Coon for “The Liberation” and Leguizamo for “The Odyssey,” are in the awards mix. Overall, Denver showcased 130 films, including many awards season favorites. Related Stories ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

I served on the documentary jury this year and awarded the Maysles Brothers Award to one of the year’s most revered docs. We chose the nonfiction portrait of adolescence “Whispers in May,” winner of this year’s CPH:DOX and from Chinese filmmaker Dongnan Chen, which is still seeking distribution. Per our statement penned with Vanity Fair’s Chris Murphy and producer Justine Suzanne Jones as fellow jurors, it’s “a vivid and compassionate portrait of female friendship in the twilight of adolescence” and “formally daring and emotionally authentic.” Other films in the category included “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” “Nuisance Bear,” and “SUMO: Spirit Weighs Nothing.”

Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra,” which just won the BFI London Film Festival audience award after winning that same prize at TIFF in September, won the Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film. The Spanish epic about gay desire and Federico García Lorca is locked in for multiple Oscar nominations at this point, with its awards streak going back to Best Director at Cannes in May.

The Audience Award for narrative feature, just as it did at the Virginia Film Festival in October, went to Peter Farrelly’s Sly Stallone behind-the-scenes biopic “I Play Rocky.” The film, starring charming breakout Anthony Ippolito as the “Rocky” star/screenwriter, was the runner-up to “La Bola Negra” in Toronto’s audience award category. “I Play Rocky” is in select theaters Thursday ahead of a November 20 wide release, and its popularity as an audience favorite is proving hard to best at fests.

See the full list of Denver Film Festival winners below.

#3591. ‘Dexter: Resurrection’s Michael C. Hall Teases a Dark New Twist to Dexter’s Formula

Editor’s Note: The following contains spoilers for Dexter: Resurrection Season 2, Episode 2

What does a midlife crisis look like for a serial killer? Well, if you’re Dexter Morgan, it involves listening to self-help podcasts and questioning your life’s work after nobody really appreciates all the people you’ve killed. And that’s the biggest pickle in Season 2 of Dexter: Resurrection, which finds Michael C. Hall’s antihero at a rather strange crossroads. He’s getting older, his son is a cop, and even the ghost of his dead father Harry (James Remar) thinks he’s lost his way. But as Episode 2’s “Young Blood” underscores, Dexter’s biggest problem might be his growing need for a little recognition.

In an exclusive interview with Collider, Hall reveals that Dexter is beginning to question his legacy: “He’s really wondering what it’s all worth, if it’s his secret, and the fact of his secret dies with every victim.” It's a dangerous shift for someone who’s spent most of his life trying to stay out of law enforcement’s spotlight, especially when he encounters Brian Cox’s Don Framt, the suspected New York Ripper, who seems to enjoy every bit of attention he gets.

Cox, meanwhile, explains how Don has no such reservations about his reputation. “He basks in the glory that maybe he is a serial killer, even though he knows he is a serial killer, but he basks in that glory. So he gets off on that.” It’s a rather unsettling contrast between two killers who have spent years getting away with murder, especially now that Dexter is starting to wonder whether keeping everything a secret is really worth it.

And as if Dexter didn’t have enough on his plate, Joey Quinn (Desmond Harrington) is back, looking for answers about Angel Batista’s (David Zayas) death. Speaking with Collider, Hall and Cox, alongside Harrington, Remar, and Ntare Guma Mbaho Mwine, opened up about Dexter’s changing priorities, the people complicating his life, and why his latest choices (like collaborating with Uma Thurman’s Charley) could spell serious trouble as Season 2 unfolds.

Dexter has spent a majority of his years alone, but the second episode of Season 2 finds him reconsidering a strange business proposition from Thurman’s Charley, who returns with an offer to help him track down serial killers alongside the perk of a luxury apartment. His first target? Ray Ballard (Gabriel Luna), better known as the Sleepy-Eyed Killer, who creeps into unsuspecting homes and rearranges their belongings as a form of psychological torment until he finally kills them. Naturally, Dexter has conditions of his own, but according to Hall, there’s something about Charley’s offer he finds particularly hard to resist.

“I think it’s practical, logistical reasons. She gives him access that he wouldn’t otherwise have. And on a level that maybe he can’t fully appreciate or cop to, she sees him for who he is, and as much as she can admires him for it, and he craves that,” he says. But Dexter isn’t exactly taking advice from anyone these days, including Harry. When his father questions his decisions, Dexter pushes back, even asking why he can’t just “be happy for once.” Hall admits there’s a rebellious streak emerging in his character as he gets older, describing it as “a sort of free-floating defiance that he puts on his son, on his internalized father.”

That attitude makes Dexter’s encounter with Don Framt all the more interesting. After following him to a strip club, Dexter approaches the suspected New York Ripper pretending to be an admirer. But unlike Dexter, Don doesn’t seem particularly worried about being associated with his crimes. In fact, Cox explains that the killer’s confidence comes from his impulsive nature. “The thing about it is that he’s very ignorant, also, about certain things, and he doesn’t realize that he is walking on a tightrope sometimes,” he says. “He just gets on that tightrope, and he walks it. And I think that that’s to do with the sort of spontaneous nature of who he is.”

Cox also has a rather colorful description of Don’s appetite for attention: “It’s like he’s a bit of a — excuse my bad language — self-fame fucker, if you can imagine that,” he laughs. “That’s really what he is.”

Interestingly, Cox sees a clear parallel between the two killers, especially when it comes to how long they’ve evaded consequences. “Because of the length of the show, which is interesting, the 20-year length of the show, there is that same kind of lens in the relationship of Framt getting away with it, and it’s so many, many years later. So there’s that parallel, that’s very clear in the story.”

As Dexter is busy making deals with Charley, his relationship with son Harrison (Jack Alcott) is no doubt entering some rather strange territory. Now working homicide alongside Detective Wallace (Kadia Saraf), Harrison wants his father to leave the New York Ripper alone. Of course, Dexter agrees — on the surface. In his own mind? Not so much. According to Hall, there’s a reason Dexter is having such a hard time taking orders from his own kid.

“He wants it to have been his decision and his gift that he’s given Harrison, not his command that he’s following, which I think is something — it’s obviously a unique situation, but in a father-son dynamic, something that would happen. ‘I don’t want to believe I’m following your orders, but that I’m granting you a wish you might have,’” Hall says, further warning that their unusual arrangement might not last much longer. “It’s the beginning of a thorny relationship where they’re sort of negotiating who gets to have who and who gets to kill who. I think we’d be reasonable to suspect that that’s not a sustainable dynamic.”

For Remar, who plays Dexter’s late father Harry and his conscience, his character has become an important source of support as Dexter tries to navigate fatherhood alongside his increasingly complicated personal crisis. “I serve as his anchor, and I serve as his safe harbor, because I’m the one person that knows everything about him. Even though I’m not there anymore, so to speak, I am the one person who knows everything about him.”

Meanwhile, Mwine, who plays Dexter’s neighbor Blessing, teased that their friendship could also take an unexpected turn. “Blessing brings blessings to Dexter. He also becomes a friend, and sometimes a friend needs to tell you harsh truths about yourself, challenge you to get out of your comfort zone, open new doors, be a sounding board,” he says. “These and some other dark things might unfold this season for Blessing and Dexter.”

And then there’s Harrington’s Joey Quinn, who’s back in New York looking for answers about Batista’s death. The actor, who appeared in Seasons 3 to 8 of Dexter, admits Quinn might be another obstacle the show’s titular character has to worry about, joking, “It could be that I’m in his way, or pain, or whatever.”

With so many people pulling Dexter in different directions, Hall offered one final warning about what’s coming: “More and more plates will continue to spin, and eventually all come crashing down.”

Dexter: Resurrection Season 2 streams every Friday on Paramount+ in the U.S.

#3590. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.
