#3569. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

#3568. Marvel Officially Announces Major Revamp of Classic Team, All New Members and Powers

Marvel just announced that the demonic Mephisto has assembled his own Sinister Six roster, unleashing them against the Avengers in upcoming issues of the newly launched Avengers Volume 10.

The Sinister Six debuted in 1964, when Doctor Octopus united Electro, Mysterio, Sandman, Vulture and Kraven the Hunter into a team to take down their mutual enemy, Spider-Man. Since then, there have been countless versions of the team, with a variety of members and rosters.

Now, a new Sinister Six will rise, making the team name more literal than ever before. Each member is a dead hero who made a deal with Mephisto in the past, summoned from the afterlife to do his bidding.

Mephisto is an ancient embodiment of evil who rules over Marvel's most traditional form of 'Hell,' reveling in corrupting the innocent and collecting souls. Recent issues of Captain America have seen Mephisto overthrown by Doctor Doom, who has taken his place as Hell's leader, winning the loyalty of his demonic legions.

In Captain America #16 - from Chip Zdarsky, Valerio Schiti, Romulo Fajardo Jr. and Joe Caramagna - Doom made the reckless move of canceling all Mephisto's past contracts. While this allowed Doom to solidify his rule of Hell, it also seemingly triggered a cosmic process where 'angels' arrived to reverse the effects of all Mephisto's deals - including Spider-Man's Aunt May still being alive.

Meanwhile, Mephisto has also been searching out those who made deals in the past and claiming their hearts for unknown reasons. With Avengers Armageddon predicting that a victorious Mephisto would kill Spider-Man, it seems like he's making a play for infernal power, with his new Sinister Six as his enforcers.

Notably, the 2025 Bring on the Bad Guys series revealed that across Marvel history, villains including Abomination and the Green Goblin have made deals with Mephisto, explaining why he's able to summon them as his Sinister Six. Given these villains are all dead in canon, it's possible that Avengers plans to use this storyline to permanently return at least a few of them to life.

Wolverine's nemesis, Sabretooth was killed in 2024's Wolverine Volume 7 #50 (Benjamin Percy, Victor LaValle, Geoff Shaw, Cory Smith et al.) The villain was beheaded by Wolverine (wielding the Muramasa Blade) at the conclusion of the 'Sabretooth War' arc, having killed Logan's son Akihiro and protégé Quentin Quire.

Sabretooth's ghost has been seen before now, with Marvel going to surprising lengths to confirm that he is truly, officially dead. He possesses immense strength, vicious claws and a healing factor that - at times - has been shown to overpower Wolverine's own.

Front and center in Marco Checchetto's cover for The Avengers #4, it seems like Sabretooth may be the field leader for this new Sinister Six. He's the most likely member to be permanently resurrected as a result of this story.

The Abomination died way back in 2008's Hulk Volume 2 #1 (Jeph Loeb, Ed McGuinness et al.), murdered by General Ross' Red Hulk in an act of vengeance for his daughter Betty. Over the last two decades, Abomination has returned multiple times, but always in temporary or unstable forms, repeatedly forced back into death by everyone from Marlo Chandler to the short-lived Gamma Flight team.

Abomination's debt to Mephisto seemingly goes back to 1985's Secret Wars II, though fans believed that debt had been paid by Blonsky killing Akeyo Mokinyo in Bring on the Villains. Perhaps he made another deal, or perhaps Mephisto isn't so easy to escape. After Sabretooth, he's the next most likely to get a permanent resurrection in this story.

The only being on Earth whose base strength is higher than that of the Hulk, Abomination is the team's powerhouse, and even by himself is a reason to consider this the strongest Sinister Six roster yet.

The only returning member of the original Sinister Six, Kraven died in 2019's Amazing Spider-Man Volume 5 #22 (Nick Spencer, Humberto Ramos et al.) and was replaced by his near-identical clone son of the same name. The original Kraven died willingly, passing on his legacy, and is likely to be incredibly angry to be forced back to life.

Having treated his body with various potions and drugs, Kraven is superhumanly strong and agile, possessing a total mastery of most forms of weaponry.

The serial-killer son of Venom is one of Marvel's deadliest villains, able to shapeshift into nearly any form (but preferring vicious, bladed weaponry.) However, unlike the other entries on this list, Carnage is technically alive in current canon.

The newly relaunched Spider-Woman Volume 9 (from Dan Watters, Andrea Broccardo, Mattia Iacono and Joe Sabino) has revealed that Jessica Drew is the current host of Carnage, though the symbiote's mind was mostly fried by events in recent issues of Amazing Spider-Man: Spider-Versity. Meanwhile, Cletus Cassady is stalking Jessica as a ghost-like 'codex' being.

It's likely Cletus who will be resurrected by Mephisto and granted the powers he possessed as Carnage, probably without the symbiote actually in tow.

Spider-Man's nemesis rounds out this team while acting as its biggest question mark. That's because the original Green Goblin, Norman Osborn, is still alive and well. Indeed, better than 'well' - his sins were purged back in 2020, removing the Green Goblin persona and leaving him consumed by guilt for his former villainy.

Norman has been a hero ever since, operating as both the Gold Goblin and the Resolute Spider-Man, while also supporting Peter Parker's heroism with gadgets and upgraded equipment. Of course, there have been many other Green Goblins, including Norman's son Harry Osborn, Phil Urich and Bart Hamilton, but none seem fit to stand alongside such big-name teammates.

There's another possibility: this could be the Goblin persona itself, given physical form. Modern Marvel comics treat the Green Goblin as a distinct persona within Norman Osborn. After passing between various hosts (including the Goblin Queen and Peter Parker himself), this entity was exorcised, and so would be a candidate to be 'resurrected' even without Norman.

Avengers Volume 10 is slowly but steadily bringing a new team together, following the traditional team disbanding in Avengers Armageddon. The new roster includes Spider-Man, Wolverine, Luke Cage, a weakened Captain Marvel and new hero Miracleman. In a surprise addition, the team is also being aided by junior mystic Paige Howley.

Spider-Man and Wolverine have the most obvious connections to Mephisto's Sinister Six, but Daredevil and Luke Cage have faced most of them at one time or another. While these villains would traditionally be minor threats to Carol Danvers, Avengers Armageddon saw her reduced to just 10% of her former power, making several of them potent threats.

​Notably, this makes Miracleman the only hero who could hope to contend with the Abomination. With strength and durability comparable to the Sentry, Miracleman is nevertheless mostly untested with his new powers, and couldn't stop Red Hulk's recent rampage in which thousands died. It's also worth noting that in World War Hulk, Hulk narrowly beat Sentry in a physical fight, and Abomination is traditionally even stronger.

As Mephisto's plans near their conclusion, the Avengers will be forced to contend with a brand new Sinister Six made up of classic villains, presenting the team with the first real test of their teamwork and abilities.

#3567. John Ternus addresses iPhone Duo supply constraints, display issue

Today Apple reported record Q4 earnings, which beat Wall Street expectations overall. And in an interview with Reuters, CEO John Ternus addressed current iPhone Duo supply constraints and also referenced units that have been returned for display issues.

Apple’s latest quarterly earnings did not include any sales for the iPhone Duo. That’s because it covered a period running July-September, and the Duo didn’t go on sale until October.

But Wall Street is understandably still very curious about how sales for the foldable are going. Especially as relates to revenue forecasts for the current quarter.

In an interview with Reuters, Ternus addressed two aspects of the iPhone Duo: supply constraints and units that have had display issues.

Regarding supply, it sounds like Apple doesn’t know when it might reach supply-demand balance:

“Duo is constrained as of today,” Ternus said. “The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we’re not ‌able to ⁠predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Currently, shipping estimates from the Apple Store are still set for late January. That’s where they’ve stayed since the first pre-orders immediately sold out on October 16.

On the matter of iPhone Duo screens cracking, Ternus was brief and essentially repeated what Apple had previously confirmed: that the issue is real, but limited to a very small number of units.

Ternus told Reuters that “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duo units had been returned with display issues. Apple is replacing those units with new models.

#3566. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3565. Rosamund Pike Starring in Body Horror Film ‘Feed’ for ‘Star Wars: The Acolyte’ Creator Leslye Headland

Rosamund Pike will star in and produce “Feed,” a body horror film from “Russian Doll” co-creator and “Star Wars: The Acolyte” creator Leslye Headland.

The film follows a desperate mother who discovers an obscure collagen supplement that promises to transform her tween gymnast daughter into an influencer. Fame hits fast, but as her daughter goes viral, she undergoes a terrifying transformation. “Feed” was inspired by a 2022 Finnish horror film, “Hatching.” Daniella Isaacs (“People Who Knew Me”) wrote the script.

Headland made her feature debut in 2012 with an adaptation of her play, “Bachelorette.” In 2015, she wrote and directed “Sleeping With Other People.” Both premiered at the Sundance Film Festival. Related Stories Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times Why ASMR Invaded the Soundscape of ‘La Bola Negra’

Pike was nominated for an Oscar for “Gone Girl.” Her other credits include “Saltburn,” “An Education,” and the James Bond film, “Die Another Day.” She won an Olivier Award for “Inter Alia,” a role she is reprising this fall on Broadway.

“Long have I wanted to make a film that plays anarchically with our obsession with social media and self-improvement, our desire for fame without notable admirable skill and, let’s put it out there, the monstrosity of modern motherhood,” Pike said in a statement. “‘Feed’ deals with all these things. It tracks a Momfluencer, Erin, bent on her daughter’s domination of the digital space. Erin believes that success here will protect her daughter from the horrors of our fickle world… won’t it? ‘Feed’ examines appetite. The dark appetite of online communities; the appetite of a social media landscape that monetizes youth and beauty; the appetite of a mother for her daughter’s success; and the appetite of a teenage girl, hungry for fame, self-empowerment and dominance in her relationship with her single mother. ‘Feed’ is film that plays in the genre space, and plays into our current fears, as parents, as citizens, of the digital world.”

Headland added: “Daniella’s script is audacious, disturbing and deeply human, and Rosamund is among the boldest actors working today. I couldn’t ask for better partners to take on the darker corners of this story and I feel incredibly lucky to be making this film with two women whose work I admire so much.”

The Veterans is overseeing the international sales rights, with CAA Media Finance tackling the U.S. sales. Talks will kick off next week at the American Film Market.

Pike will produce through her Primitive Streak banner, alongside Shelley Browning for Magnolia Entertainment, Steven Schneider for Spooky Pictures, Ara Keshishian and Petr Jakl for ZQ Entertainment, and Sam Ritzenberg for Agile Films. ZQ Entertainment financed the development of the script.

Pike is repped by CAA, United Agents and Magnolia Entertainment; Headland is repped by CAA and Sugar23; Isaacs is repped by Curtis Brown Group.

#3564. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3563. Apple spent a record $45.77 billion on R&D in fiscal 2026, up 32%

Apple’s research and development expenses reached a new all-time high in fiscal 2026, climbing 32% year over year to $45.77 billion. Here are the details.

While it may have taken Apple longer than some wished it had to ramp up R&D in the face of growing competition in AI, the company has significantly accelerated its spending over the past year.

As Apple shared in its Q4 2026 results, it spent $11.73 billion on R&D, bringing its total spending for fiscal 2026 to $45.77 billion, a 32% increase compared to the $34.55 billion it spent in fiscal 2025.

During an earnings call earlier this year, former CEO Tim Cook said Apple was “clearly investing more,” adding that R&D was “accelerating much higher than the company” overall. CFO Kevan Parekh also explained that AI-related spending was being added to the investments Apple was already making in its existing product roadmap.

Interestingly, today’s figures also suggest that Apple’s R&D spending may be starting to level off.

While Apple’s Q4 2026 R&D expenses were up 32% from $8.87 billion in the year-ago quarter, they were virtually unchanged from Q3, increasing by just $1 million. As the chart above shows, Apple’s R&D spending jumped significantly at the beginning of fiscal 2026, but has since stabilized at a much higher level than in previous years.

#3562. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Earlier this week, one of the most intense shows on Netflix made its explosive return after two years away. Black Doves stars Keira Knightley as Helen Webb, who is placed under the protection of an old friend (Ben Whishaw) after her husband, the UK's Secretary of State for Defence (Andrew Buchan), is murdered.

Following a must-watch first season, the second is ready to turn up the tension dial. "Helen is still betraying her nation’s secrets to the covert organization she serves," according to a second-season synopsis, although "she’s walking a more treacherous line than ever" as her husband prepares to become Prime Minister. Writer Joe Barton's stylish, detailed spy thriller dazzled audiences in 2024 and will do so again this weekend.

Created by Stacey Aglok MacDonald and Alethea Arnaquq-Baril, the Canadian comedy North of North has been one of Netflix's best hidden gems since it debuted last year. Earlier this week, the second season arrived, so now is the best time to catch up on what you might have missed, as young Inuk woman Siaja (Anna Lambe) reinvents her image after a public breakup.

Easy to watch and packed with heartfelt comedy, North of North isn't the most demanding series available on Netflix, thriving as comfort viewing for its many fans. Maika Harper, Braeden Clarke, Bailey Poching, and more also star alongside Lambe in this Canadian favorite, which scored a perfect 100% rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes after its first season.

#3558. Inside ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’: How an R Rating, Filming in IMAX, and Epic Kaiju Battles Broke Franchise Tradition

[Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Godzilla Minus Zero.”]

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is gnarlier (it well earns the franchise’s first R-rating) and more cantankerous in its sound design. Still, any fears that the follow-up to 2023’s beloved “Godzilla Minus One” would sacrifice spectacle for sentiment can rest at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean.

Director Takashi Yamazaki returns to direct, write, and aid in the VFX work on his kaiju clobberfest, which is set two years later, focusing on the family comprised of former kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter, Akiko (Sae Nagatani), as they attempt to resume normal life in the aftermath of Godzilla’s attack. While Shikishima’s allies such as Kenji Oda (Hidetaka Yoshioka) have used the tragedy as a springboard to rebuild against all odds, the arrival of a dragon-like beast threatens to dismantle the short-lived peace. Shikishima and his allies try their best to combat the extraterrestrial threat while debating whether Godzilla is worth the risk of resurrection, acknowledging that sometimes the only way to beat one kaiju is with another. Related Stories Rosamund Pike Starring in Body Horror Film ‘Feed’ for ‘Star Wars: The Acolyte’ Creator Leslye Headland Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times

With this film, Yamazaki burrows into the pointed theme of survivor’s guilt that has characterized his two (and hopefully counting) takes on Godzilla, through new characters like Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) and Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), exploring how greeting a new day can feel like its own penance. Indeed, how this film plays with Japan’s atomic grievances, tapping into a generation’s latent rage and the notion that opportunity is just tragedy that has shed its skin, feels like a culmination of 30-plus years of storytelling with the character. After watching all the “Godzilla” films this year in anticipation of this one, I can say that “Godzilla Minus Zero” rewards ardent fans of the franchise by building on certain mythologies while cleverly subverting others. Furthermore, it complicates our relationship to the catharsis of a good creature clash by presenting meekness, restraint, and peacekeeping with their own reverential power.

After the movie’s premiere at this year’s New York Film Festival, where the sounds of scorched earth, smelted scrap metal, and kaiju roars rattled in my brain, I tried my best to unravel Yamazaki’s monster mayhem, where, in a spoiler-filled chat, we discussed the influence of “The Thing”, “Intolerance”, and “Close Encounters of the Third Kind”, how the historical fluidity of Godzilla’s greatest foe proved apt for the film’s thematic provocations around adaptation and rebirth, and the creative possibilities that working with IMAX sound and scale afforded him.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length. It was conducted via translator.

IndieWire: “Godzilla Minus Zero” breaks the franchise tradition in two key ways: It’s the first Japanese production filmed in IMAX and the first to carry an R rating. How did those production choices help you tell the story the way you wanted?

Takashi Yamazaki: During pre-production and even production, we had conversations with our team that, yes, extreme visual representation or going about the visual expression of the film in the way we were thinking could risk our rating. But I felt, especially for the themes that we were exploring and tackling, to properly communicate that, we could not run away from an R rating. So yes, of course I’d love for kids and families to be able to see this film, but when I weighed everything on a scale between going for the rating and possibly editing or censoring what the message was supposed to be, going all in on conveying this vision won out.

Where we really see the rating apply is in focusing on the bodies that have been charred and incinerated by atomic bombs and Godzilla’s atomic breath.

I could see other films benefiting from more abstracted visual expression or at least visuals that are a bit more sugarcoated, but I did not think that was the case for this film. It was important to show it all in a direct manner.

On the note of IMAX, you used actual aircraft to record engine noises and played monster roars in a mountain dam to capture the acoustics of the kaiju roars. How did the IMAX technology impact your approach to crafting the film’s sonic landscape?

When people hear the term “IMAX,” the focus tends to be on the visual aspects and the imagery. While that’s fair, IMAX’s capacity to express various sounds and create a sonic experience is quite amazing and underrated. When the team and I decided to film “Godzilla Minus Zero” in IMAX, we watched a lot of films to prepare, and no matter the film, I remember walking away from my experiences feeling very shaken to my core. I wanted to evoke that same emotion. When the kaiju roar in this film, I wanted the audience to experience a very real sense of fear. I think back to when we were monkeys and predators would chase after us. That’s the type of fear I wanted people to experience, that sense of being out in the wild and feeling tense because you hear the roar of something that would chase after and eat you.

In a lot of ways, I think the sonic threat is greater than the visual threat back in the day when we would meet predators. When we took the kaiju sounds to record in the dam and hit it with the sound, we wanted to specifically record how those sounds bounced around the environment, into the trees, into the atmosphere. I think what that process did for us is that it took these fantastical creatures and brought them into the real world. Before you see the kaiju, you hear them, not unlike how we might have run from predators when we were monkeys.

What specific animal sounds did you use to craft the roar of the newest kaiju you introduced, Ghidorah?

We looked at various libraries and tapped into some older Ghidorah recordings and then mixed those with recordings of animals such as deer, hawk, tiger, and even some human voices. I wanted to keep the image of the original Ghidorah but add a modern interpretation to it, and something is fitting about Ghidorah’s roar being this amalgamation of all these different creatures. There were various roars we auditioned, but once again, it had to work on an acoustic level, which is where testing the sounds in the dam came in.

You introduce several new characters, and I found myself most compelled by Min Tanaka’s Kanji Murakami. He courses with righteous fury and trauma but does not know how to channel it into anything but revenge. What drew you to craft the emotional spine of this movie around this?

For me, I would say that thematic backbone would be about the twin poles of human foolishness and arrogance. When you look at Murakami’s ideology and actions, I don’t think he thought about what would come after his revenge was actualized. What was on the other side of his actions? What new hate would that create? I think his story, in part, is the story of human history: how acting on hate leads to a chain of events that keeps spiraling onward. On an individual level, we come face to face with a moment where human action can do something, and that was what I wanted to see through his character.

Looking at Godzilla at large and what gave birth to Godzilla, this film is really a reflection of that era. I think at the time of those earlier films, there was a huge fear of what nuclear warfare could mean. People were seriously grappling with this question of “Are we going to go into war again?” That was an anxious tension when Godzilla was born and a byproduct of the sentiment. Those anxieties are very much the fabric of the social context of the people. Exploring Hiroshima was central to “Godzilla Minus Zero” for that reason, but also, in incorporating that history into the main drama of this film, I hope that it hints at how we break the cycle that has defined human history and go in a more hopeful direction.

Focusing a bit more on the kaiju, you previously described making a kaiju film as kagura … “a dance to please and calm the gods, where you place these problems into the shape of a kaiju to help process some of these worries, almost like a ceremony.” You have two “shapes” here with Ghidorah and Godzilla. What were you trying to fill them with?

I think there’s always a dance that happens whenever a “Godzilla” movie is made. It is almost as though the filmmaker and creative team are trying to quell something. The Godzilla movie in and of itself becomes an offering to the gods.

Every time I feel a “Godzilla” movie is released, there’s some sort of imbalance that’s happening in human society that Godzilla is course-correcting. Looking at the two kaiju that are battling it out and sort of what they embody in this film, Godzilla has been spoken about at length in that he originated from this idea and fear of nuclear weapons and the overall terror of war. We have something a bit more abstract in Ghidorah; he is this unknown terror that comes from the sky. So we have, on one hand, war, and on the other hand, terror that comes from the sky. I think the fact that mankind has to rely on war, they have to borrow its power to quell something else, is interesting; it’s almost as if they have to tap into a forbidden realm for salvation given their circumstances.

Ghidorah has always been a kaiju that can adapt — I think of how he becomes Mecha King Ghidorah in Kazuki Ōmori’s 1991 “Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah” — and here, his power set includes assimilating genetic material. It feels fitting given Ghidorah’s powers in past films, but where did this idea originate?

In terms of the look of how Ghidorah “assimilates,” I was quite inspired by John Carpenter’s “The Thing,” where the creature absorbs its surroundings and then turns it into a part of itself. It cannot be divorced from the environment it is in. That feels in line with Ghidorah. For the very first form of Ghidorah as well, I wanted to pay homage to Hedorah, particularly in how it sort of “consumes” and how it moves.

“Godzilla vs. Hedorah” is probably my favorite Shōwa film. Watching Godzilla and Ghidorah fight made me think of Ishirō Honda’s “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster,” because of the famous fight between those two where they use the environment — such as boulders — to fight. You incorporate Ghidorah’s gravity beam in this film, which can turn a city into ruins and then turn those ruins into weapons. Talk about including the environment more in these fight sequences you crafted.

That’s interesting. Perhaps that final fight could be seen as a reinterpretation for modern audiences of what Honda was doing in his film. Overall, I did feel the idea of the environment itself being a part of the clash or “joining in on the fight” was interesting. When the monsters fight, it’s not in a vacuum; there’s always collateral. For Ghidorah, I talked with the team about how his gravity beam — despite being called that–has not been seen taking advantage of gravity in a way onscreen before. I thought tapping into that would make for a very interesting visual element for these fights.

You’ve also cited Alfonso Cuarón’s “Children of Men” as an inspiration, and the influence shows in the film’s opening with Ghidorah and in the dogfight scene. Why did you feel the language of “long takes” was necessary for these scenes?

These longer shots give a very almost claustrophobic feel where you can’t escape your environment. There was a long take in the middle of Cuarón’s film, where we track a soldier who has to climb upstairs and fight his way up and out of this town that’s become a battlefield. There is no respite in the form of a cut. That had a huge impression on me because through that technique, Cuarón made it so that, as an audience member, even if I wanted to, I could not escape; I could only carry out the mission or die.

In kaiju movies, when there’s a kaiju attack, you can use cuts to either cut to a scene where someone successfully escapes or cut to a scene where they die. There are really only two options. You can create a different dramatic sensation that complicates that binary by having these long takes where these characters are saying, “I have to face this; I have to do something about what’s in front of me because there is no escape.”

Ultimately, I wanted to give the audience this feeling of being unable to escape from a Kaiju, but also because you’re in a movie theater, you also can’t escape from watching that as well. What Cuarón crafted with “Children of Men,” I wanted to create but with a kaiju lens.

To bring up another cinematic reference, you mentioned that D.W. Griffith’s film “Intolerance” inspired you. With this film, you wanted to create a story where “If a small family can attain a small happiness, the world will be OK.”

I believe that the path to happiness around the world is the collective happiness of the individual. “Intolerance” explores this lack of empathy among people. In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” I think this very small happiness in the Shikishima family unit–a unit which is the smallest unit in society–is poignant; despite the tragedies happening around them, if there is even a glimmer of hope and happiness that this very small unit of mankind can bond with each other and be present, perhaps that means all of us can be one step closer to achieving more of the same. So much of this movie deals with “infection,” but in seeing the Shikishima not only cheering that happiness but allowing it to grow even amidst wartime, I think that can be contagious and hopefully spread to their neighbors, and then larger units of society.

GKIDS releases “Godzilla Minus Zero” in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3557. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3556. Apple says memory costs and Siri AI will weigh on holiday quarter profit margins

Following today’s earnings report, Apple held its quarterly earnings call, during which the company discussed the impact of rising memory costs on its profit margins and warned of additional pressure from Siri AI expenses during the holiday quarter. Here are the details.

Over the past few quarters, Apple has repeatedly warned that rising component costs would put pressure on its profit margins. Last quarter, gross margin was 50.1%, up from 49.3% in Q2. However, that included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.

Today, Apple reported that its gross margin fell to 47.9% in Q4 2026, with product gross margin dropping to 37.2%, down from 40.1% in the previous quarter. That represented a 2.2-percentage-point decline in company-wide gross margin and a 2.9-percentage-point drop in product gross margin.

Against the backdrop of record September quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh explained that tariff refunds once again provided some relief, though not enough to offset the impact of rising memory costs. He also noted that, excluding the impact of tariff refunds, the sequential decline in gross margins would have been roughly one percentage point, primarily due to higher memory costs:

“We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs.”

Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon, with the company forecasting gross margins of between 45% and 46% for Q1 2027.

He attributed the expected decline primarily to higher memory costs, alongside the impact of the ongoing Siri AI rollout.

When asked to elaborate, Parekh explained that Siri AI will affect Apple’s margins in two ways. First, running the service will increase cloud costs. Second, Apple will have to spread out the recognition of some revenue from devices that include Siri AI over their lifetimes, rather than counting it all at the time of sale.

This, he added, is an accounting practice Apple already follows for other services bundled with its devices, such as Maps, Siri, and iCloud:

“Consistent with how we’ve always accounted for Maps, Siri, and iCloud, for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device.”

Meanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter.

Ternus said recent price increases across the Mac, iPad, and iPhone lineups would help offset some of those costs, alongside existing inventory purchased at lower prices and savings on certain non-memory components. He also warned that the benefits of carrying lower-cost memory inventory would diminish over time. Apple did not say whether it expects to raise product prices yet again to compensate.

#3555. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3554. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3553. Apple forecasts its biggest revenue quarter ever despite supply constraints

During today’s earnings call following its fiscal Q4 2026 report, Apple said it expects its December quarter “to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.” Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with revenue climbing 12% year over year to $114.5 billion and net profit reaching $30.71 billion. This marked September-quarter records on both fronts, despite supply constraints on iPhone, Mac, and iPad, as well as rising memory costs.

During the conference call following the earnings report, Apple acknowledged that higher memory costs were putting pressure on its profit margins, while also warning of limited supply-chain flexibility, stronger-than-expected demand for Mac and iPad, and ongoing shortages of the new iPhone Duo.

Still, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh was very clear about what the company expects from the next fiscal quarter, which includes the holiday shopping season:

We expect our December quarter total company revenue to grow between 7 and 10% year over year, which reflects our best view of constrained supply. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.

If this pans out, Apple’s fiscal Q1 2027 revenue should fall between $153.82 billion and $158.13 billion, adding between $10 billion and $14.4 billion in revenue compared to the year-ago quarter.

Beyond revenue, Parekh also shared Apple’s expectations for several other financial metrics during the December quarter:

Parekh noted that “third-party licensing and foreign exchange” will be the primary headwinds for the Services revenue, while higher memory costs and “some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI” are expected to put further pressure on the company’s gross margins.

Finally, Apple cautioned that its outlook “assumes that global tariff rates, policies, and their application remain in effect as of this call, and the global macroeconomic outlook does not worsen from today.“

#3552. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3551. Karin Slaughter's New 5/5 Thriller Series Officially Debuts Next Week

Lade Omotade is a News and Features Author at Collider, covering everything from casting announcements and streaming trends to behind-the-scenes stories and the cultural impact of today's biggest film and TV franchises. Since joining the team in 2024, she has written more than 1,000 news stories, with her work also cited by outlets like AOL and IMDb.

Karin Slaughter is back with another suspenseful thriller adapted for television, officially debuting next week. Widely recognized for her dark, gripping crime novels that have sold more than 40 million copies worldwide, Slaughter is a #1 New York Times and Sunday Times bestselling author of over 25 books published in 120 countries. One of her most popular thrillers is the Will Trent series, adapted for small screens in 2023, starring Ramón Rodríguez in the titular role, andnow in its 4th season on ABC.

Will Trent isn't the only Slaughter adaptation on TV, as another similarly thrilling one is Pieces of Her. Based on her 2018 standalone novel, Pieces of Her was adapted into an eight-episode TV series. It stars Toni Collette and Bella Heathcote and premiered on March 4, 2022. Upon release, the gripping series debuted at #1 worldwide on Netflix, and between February 27, 2022, and April 3, 2022, it was watched 227.5 million hours globally on the streamer.

Four years later, another Slaughter crime thriller launches on TV as a limited series starring Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy. Titled The Good Daughter, this twisty mystery series officially premieres on Peacock on November 12, 2026, with all six one-hour episodes exclusively available to stream at once. Slaughter wrote every episode and serves as showrunner, with the iconic Steph Green, Emmy-nominated in 2020 for Best Director for the Watchmen episode "Little Fear of Lightning," directing the adaptation.

Initially, Slaughter wasn't keen on The Good Daughter adaptation when asked to write the series, but she eventually became curious about the screenwriting process. "I chose The Good Daughter because it's always been one of my favorite books," the author told Peacock.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Adapted from Slaughter's 2017 novel, The Good Daughter is a standalone story with a beginning, middle, and end that tells what happened to the Quinn family of Pikeville, Georgia. It sees Byrne and Fahy as estranged sisters, Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, who, as kids, witnessed a traumatic incident that badly impacted their family. Sam was left injured, and she eventually moved far away from home.

Twenty years later, another violent crime shakes the sisters' Georgia hometown, prompting Sam to return home. Charlotte, who follows in her father's footsteps by working in town as a lawyer, is the first witness on the scene. This stirs up traumatic memories of what happened to her and her sister years ago, and they're both forced to confront what happened. Also starring in the miniseries are Brendan Gleeson, Paula Malcomson, Jake McDorman, and Olivia Williams.

The Good Daughter premieres next week on Peacock. Watch the official trailer above.
