#3550. SEAL Team's Spiritual Sequel Is TV's Most-Watched Show

While the David Boreanaz vehicle SEAL Team might have wrapped up in 2024 after seven seasons, Taylor Sheridan’s biggest TV hit is a perfect replacement for the procedural series. Although there are a lot of actors who are small-screen staples, few have managed an unbroken network TV run quite as consistent and impressive as Buffy the Vampire Slayer supporting star David Boreanaz has since 1997.

Boreanaz’s role as Angel in Buffy the Vampire Slayer led to a spinoff show, Angel, and the actor starred in the murder mystery series Bones for 12 seasons after Angel’s five-season run came to a close. Once Bones ended, Boreanaz played Master Chief Special Warfare Operator Jason Hayes in CBS’s SEAL Team from 2017 until 2024. Although Boreanaz has since gone on to star in a reboot of The Rockford Files, Yellowstone creator Taylor Sheridan has provided viewers with the perfect SEAL Team replacement since the procedural series ended.

Although Yellowstone’s John Dutton might be dead and buried, the legacy of Sheridan’s five-season Neo-Western lives on in the sequel shows Dutton Ranch and Marshals. While the former is a campy drama that focuses on Beth and Rip’s power struggles at a new ranch, the latter turns Kayce’s post-Yellowstone life into a police procedural. Marshals follows Kayce’s decision to join the US Marshals after Monica’s death, and turns the Yellowstone franchise into an unlikely SEAL Team substitute in the process.

Even though SEAL Team was a conventional military police procedural influenced by the NCIS franchise and JAG, Marshals has a lot in common with the earlier CBS show. For one thing, SEAL Team show runner Spencer Hudnut is also the showrunner of Marshals, taking over from Yellowstone’s original creator Sheridan. Since Sheridan currently has a staggering 11 seasons of TV to oversee, this behind-the-scenes switch-up makes sense for the CBS show.

Since Yellowstone became a breakout success in 2018, Sheridan has parlayed the show’s popularity into a sprawling franchise consisting of Dutton Ranch, Marshals, the original series, the prequel shows 1883 and 1923, and the upcoming prequel 1944. Meanwhile, he has also written the prison drama Mayor of Kingstown, the crime comedy Tulsa King and its spinoff Frisco King, the family drama The Madison, and the spy series Lioness.

Thus, hiring Hudnut as the showrunner for Marshals was a natural evolution for the Yellowstone franchise. However, this also means that the format of the CBS procedural has more in common with SEAL Team’s setup than Yellowstone’s original storytelling style. Essentially a darker, R-rated spin on campy Western melodramas of the 80s like Dynasty and Dallas, Yellowstone was a soapy series that focused on the Dutton family’s power struggles and their internal squabbles.

In contrast, much like SEAL Team, Marshals centers on a group of law enforcement officers who work together closely in life-or-death situations. Both shows also center on complex antiheroes with military roots, thanks to Kayce’s background as a veteran. Although Marshals does continue Yellowstone’s story, its execution is far closer in style and tone to SEAL Team than the original show.

The fact that Kayce plays the role of a law enforcement officer, when the Dutton family spent the entirety of Yellowstone’s story actively fighting and flouting the law, already makes for a major story departure. However, Marshals is still very much a Yellowstone series despite its similarities to SEAL Team, and the CBS hit offers a distinctly Yellowstone-flavored spin on the police procedural setup.

For example, where a show in the NCIS franchise or SEAL Team would be more likely to focus on its entire ensemble and their dynamics, most episodes of Marshals still single out Kayce as their primary focus. His strained relationship with Tate often earns more Marshals screen time than his colleagues, meaning this Yellowstone spinoff still owes as much to its predecessor as it does to SEAL Team.

#3549. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

#3547. Apple stock drops nearly 3% after hours following Q4 2026 results

Apple shares fell as much as 4.43% in after-hours trading on Monday during the company’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, before recovering some of those losses later in the evening. Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with a 12% increase in revenue, another 12% increase in net profit, and record revenue from its Services category, following its first sequential quarterly decline in 15 quarters.

The results also included a 17% increase in iPhone revenue and a 24% increase in Mac revenue, but an 8% decline in Wearables, Home, and Accessories revenue, which Apple attributed to “a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year,” and a 10% decline in iPad revenue, which Apple attributed to supply constraints and a similarly difficult comparison against last year’s A16-powered iPad launch.

During the conference call, Apple CEO John Ternus, CFO Kevan Parekh, and COO Sabih Khan fielded questions from analysts about rising memory costs, recent hardware price increases, and ongoing supply constraints, including those affecting the iPhone Duo.

Hopefully Apple can use this aberration in trading algorithms to cancel as many shares as possible on the cheap!

The executives also offered a mixed outlook for the holiday quarter, with Apple expecting its highest quarterly revenue ever, but slower year-over-year growth, lower profit margins, and continued shortages of Mac and iPad models.

After ending the regular trading session down 1.83%, Apple shares initially climbed 0.5% to $340.00 following the earnings release. However, as the conference call progressed, the stock reversed course, falling to $323.33, or 4.43% below Monday’s closing price. Shares then recovered some of those losses, ending the after-hours session at $328.81, down 2.81%.

Of course, post-earnings after-hours trading doesn’t necessarily reflect how a stock will perform during the next day’s regular session, so it remains to be seen how investors will react when markets reopen on Tuesday after digesting tonight’s news.

#3543. Apple to require 18+ age ratings for dating apps and AI romantic companions

Apple today announced new age rating requirements coming to the App Store, covering apps with location-sharing features, as well as dating and relationship features. Here are the details.

In an update to its Developer News blog, Apple today announced that starting November 16, developers will be required to declare whether their apps include location-sharing or dating and relationship features when completing the age rating questionnaire in App Store Connect.

When completing the age rating questionnaire in App Store Connect, you’ll need to declare whether your app includes:

The company added that “apps that include Dating and Relationships receive a minimum age rating of 18+,” while “apps that include Shared Location may not have an impact on their minimum age rating in some regions.”

Apple notes that in Brazil, local regulations require an A16 rating for apps with location-sharing features and an A18 rating for those with dating and relationship features. However, developers can request a lower official rating from Brazil’s Ministry of Justice and Public Security if they believe their apps qualify, such as those designed to let parents and children share their locations.

Finally, Apple said developers must provide these declarations when submitting an app update or changing their age rating questionnaire, with all apps required to complete them by January 12, 2027.

#3542. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3541. Sydney Sweeney's The Housemaid Faces Its Biggest Test With New Stage Adaptation

Sydney Sweeney's erotic R-rated thriller is about to face a big test without her. While some of Sydney Sweeney's movies have struggled to find an audience (Madame Web, Ron Howard's Eden), she's also scored major hits too. She all but revived the long-dormant romantic comedy genre with 2023's Anyone but You, and gave erotic movie thrillers a much-needed boost thanks to The Housemaid.

This adaptation of Freida McFadden's 2022 novel casts Sweeney in the title role as an ex-con who discovers a sinister side to the rich family she's been hired by. While it lacks the more outrageous energy of something like Basic Instinct, The Housemaid is still an R-rated delight. It also gave an impressive showcase to dual leads Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried, and The Housemaid grossed $400 million worldwide (via Box Office Mojo).

Considering it cost $35 million to produce, that, of course, means a sequel is already in production with Sweeney returning. It looks like The Housemaid is on the verge of becoming a full-fledged franchise item, with Deadline revealing stage adaptation is also in the works.

The Housemaid stage play is set to arrive in September 2027, with playwright and screenwriter Bekah Brunstetter (This Is Us) handling the adaptation. The play will open at Richmond Theatre in London, but while no actors have been confirmed yet, it should go without saying that neither Sydney Sweeney nor Amanda Seyfried will be reprising their roles.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

Given the popularity of both the book series and the 2025 film, The Housemaid stage adaptation is certain to become a major draw. Now, the movie adaptation was very much sold on Sydney Sweeney's star power, which proved a safe bet considering its final box office tally. That said, it was also based on a bestselling book, and the premise held appeal to both female and male audiences.

In short, The Housemaid stage adaptation could prove that it was the property itself - and not its cast - that was the main draw. The play is set to debut a few months ahead of the release of the film sequel The Housemaid's Secret in December 2027, so it will be interesting to see how the stage version fares compared to its big screen counterpart.

If The Housemaid stage adaptation is a runaway success, it will show that the franchise itself can succeed without Sweeney. Even so, if the second entry is a hit (and it likely will be), the odds are good Sweeney will return for the trilogy capper, The Housemaid Is Watching, before moving on from the role.

It's to Sweeney's benefit to stick with the series for now. It's an R-rated franchise that gives her a great role to play, and it's a character which allows her to do both subtle work and get very hammy too. There is also safety in trying out other kinds of projects whilst having a reliable series to slip back into every few years.

Right now, Sweeney is the actor most associated with the Millie part, but that could change if the play is a smash hit and expands worldwide. That works both ways, however, as some audiences may not give the play a chance since Sweeney won't be reprising the title role. Ultimately, the existence of the play is only going to strengthen the franchise and prove it can succeed in multiple forms - even without its original lead.

Outside of the upcoming The Housemaid's Secret, Sydney Sweeney has plenty of projects to keep her busy. This includes a live-action take on the beloved anime Gundam for Netflix, alongside a modern retelling of the Sleepy Hollow legend with director Lindsey Anderson Beer's Hollow; Sweeney will also front the Kim Novak biopic Scandalous!

The Housemaid follows Millie, who takes a job as a housemaid for a wealthy couple, Nina and Andrew. While initially offering a fresh start, her position reveals the family's perilous secrets that far surpass her own challenges.

#3540. We Have ‘Blood of My Blood’s Most Despicable Villain To Thank for Eight Seasons of ’Outlander’

Editor's note: The following contains spoilers for Outlander: Blood of My Blood Season 2, Episode 8.

In Episode 8 of Season 2 of the Starz series Outlander: Blood of My Blood, entitled “The Dance,” Lord Lovat (Tony Curran) brings Julia (Hermione Corfield) to an event honoring Loyalist Lairds who fought against Jacobites in the Rebellion, which really makes him feel like he’s flying high with his newfound respect from the upper echelon. When Lovat meets Margaret Grant (Erin Shanagher) there’s an immediate attraction that proves problematic seeing as he already has a wife. Malcolm lets Lovat know that if marriage with Margaret were to happen, he’d have to get rid of Julia first, but Julia is not stupid and sees what’s developing right in front of her, leaving her to wonder whether Lovat will divorce or kill her.

Collider recently got the opportunity to chat with Curran about Lord Lovat’s peacocking and what his interest in Margaret might mean moving forward. During the interview, he discussed how vain and villainous his character is, viewing the hate mail he gets as a badge of honor, the horrible thing he did to Ellen (Harriet Slater) and his surprise at Brian’s (Jamie Roy) reaction, what Lovat hopes to gain from Margaret, and where things will go next.

Simon Fraser being called the Hero of Inverness is a change for Lord Lovat.

TONY CURRAN: Isn’t that a contradiction of terms? It’s hilarious.

Is he feeling high and mighty right now, at this moment of his life? Is he just puffed up?

CURRAN: It’s so funny. There is a clownishness and a completely ridiculous nature to this man. I get hate mail, which I take as a badge of honor. I’ve played some despicable, nasty [characters] in my time, but he’s particularly Machiavellian. He’s got an operatic floating nature to his rhetoric that the lovely writers put pen to paper to create. He’s a lot of fun to play, but he’s becoming, day by day, even more insufferable. He’s like an old dame, going to the ball. That’s the way I pictured it. He’s an old peacock. He’s a little vain, and he wants to look pretty and handsome for the other people there who are of the upper echelon.

'Outlander: Blood of My Blood' Season 2 premieres September 18 on Starz.

How does it feel to play a character that everybody is probably rooting for the demise of?

CURRAN: Yeah. It’s a lot of fun, truth be told. A lot of villains, or any character really, are a catalyst. You just don’t know what’s going to come out of his mouth or what he’s going to do next or who he’s going to do next, as it were. He’s very uncompromising and he’s very vengeful. Now he’s got a silver medal from the king, which is obviously better than a bronze medal for Malcolm. His feathers are up. He’s peacocking. His hair is done. He’s clean-shaven. He’s got these wonderful glad rags on. It feels like he’s back to where he should be, at the king’s table at the top of the pile.

It’s unforgivable what he did to Ellen, forcing her to miscarry. Whether he actually took away her ability to ever have a child or not, it’s a horrible thing to do to someone. What was your reaction to that? Do you think he ever hesitated at all about following through with it?

CURRAN: No. They’ve got me to thank for eight seasons of Outlander because, basically, it didn’t actually work. For some reason, I didn’t put enough poison in the wine because, at some juncture, my boy and Ellen do have a child, gosh darn it, and it maybe gets in the way of the prophecy. But I don’t think he ever hesitated. I think that’s what is so surprising and shocking about it. That was fun for us to play, as actors, with the nuances and the subtleties of a happy homecoming and meal with my daughter-in-law that actually has a very dark side to it and an end game, if you will, in more ways than three.

For Ellen, Harriet [Slater]’s performance was incredible as she’s losing the baby because of what Lovat did. There is a moment when Julia confronts Lovat in his bedchamber and says, “You poisoned the wine.” A lot of it was meant to be clandestine. He was going to be like, “Oh, she’s miscarried. Brian, I’m so sorry. I had her life saved, her and Grace, from that awful MacKinney man, and I brought her back, and we were waiting for you to return.” That would have been the chat. But Julia is not stupid. She noticed that I wasn’t drinking too much, although I was still a bit hazy myself. And then, I ended up saying, “You know what? Yeah, I bloody well did poison her because we need to have our son go on the throne and the prophecy must be fulfilled.” She was apoplectic that I would do such a horrendous thing.

I think there was a moment where I said to the director, “Should there be a little bit of guilt here? This is an awful bloody thing to do to a person, a woman, a womb.” And he was like, “I don’t know.” We tried to give it a little flavor of regret, but I don’t really think there was much. It gives it a bit more color. I think Lovat is very black and white. There’s no gray area with him. But when he’s playing the generous host, he gets to perform, and Lovat’s life is a performance. All the world’s a stage. As soon as he gets his medal from the king, he sees Lady Margaret as a prize. If he marries Lady Margaret, which historically, by all accounts, did happen, then that’s bigamy.

Showrunner Matthew B. Roberts and Executive Producer Maril Davis talk about the evolving relationships in Season 2 of 'Outlander: Blood of My Blood.'

What was that scene like to shoot with Jamie Roy – that moment when Lovat has the realization that this is not just a threat and that Brian actually really intends to kill his father?

CURRAN: There was a period of episodes where that had been bubbling away. Obviously, finding out what I did to Ellen, and then having that attitude of nonchalance, being like, “Well, you put your cock before your family and before your clan.” He’s always putting him down and constantly berating him and Ellen, and he’d had enough. I remember that day, Jamie was somewhat volcanic. I could see him standing in the corner. There’s a picture I have of him just standing there with his head down, and there’s his back with that incredible leather jacket and his kilt. It was just him getting ready for that. So, I knew I was in trouble. It was simmering away. But I liked the idea that it was very sudden when he came at me.

It was an exciting scene to shoot. He pushed me, way across the room. There were a lot of different ideas for that scene. Lovat tried to fight back, but he’s an older man, and this young man has just come back from fighting the Battle of Sheriffmuir, which he survived. He’s got this vengeance in his soul for what I’ve done to Ellen. Jamie was bubbling away. It definitely gets your adrenaline going. It was very exciting to shoot that scene. And then, thank God, Davina and Julia showed up or I might not have lasted the episode.

That meeting between Lovat and Margaret is so interesting because he seems to view her a little bit differently than he views most woman. He doesn’t seem to have a lot of respect for most women. What do you think it is about her that that is a little bit different for him?

CURRAN: Affluence. Erin Shanagher, who plays Lady Margaret, is a lot of fun. She’s such a breath of fresh air. You’ve got all these wonderful characters coming in, and she’s a piston. She’s a firecracker. I think Lovat really responds to that. She’s obviously affluent, or he thinks she is. She’s asking Malcolm Grant for money. He’s a little smitten with her. She definitely catches his eye. Obviously, anything to get one up on Malcolm Grant. Although Malcolm suggests that they get together, he doesn’t really like it when they actually get together. He’s like, “Get a room!,” when they’re canoodling in a stairwell. He’s social climbing, old Lovat, and he’s gotten to a perch now that he likes where he is. He doesn’t want to fall back down, so she could have a real part to play in that rise.

You mentioned Julia being a smart woman, and she notices pretty quickly that something is going on with the two of them. Do you think Lovat would ever divorce her, or is he more likely to kill her than divorce her?

CURRAN: I think maybe the latter. He’ll just sweep her aside, or she’ll just disappear. That Grant girl seemed to disappear, old Seema. The whole marriage was a sham anyway, in Season 1. There’s nothing that he wouldn’t do that benefits him, and he’ll cut corners. He’s an old narcissist.

What can you say to tease what’s still to come for Lovat, after this episode? Where does he go from here?

CURRAN: He may well marry Lady Grant. And then, there’s the danger of what he’s going to do with Julia. But there’s also Brian. Are they ever going to see each other again, after what happened? I didn’t expect him to try to kill me. I thought he never would. I didn’t think he had the gonads to do what he did to me. Maybe there’s just something in Lovat’s twisted mind where he’s like, “Oh, this is great. If he could behave like this to my enemies, with this strength and passion and fire, and I could turn that on them and not me, then Brian could be very useful." Maybe in the future, Lovat could become more of a dad. It’s a dangerous game that he’s playing with Malcolm Grant, as well, siding with the crown and not the Jacobites. And then, there’s Dougal Mackenzie and the Mackenzie side of things. I betrayed him and his friend Angus died, so there may be some vengeance in the pipeline there, but I can’t say for sure.

Apple reportedly sent notifications to users in 99 countries warning of potential mercenary spyware attacks, as German authorities investigate reports that lawmakers and government officials may have been targeted. Here are the details.

A couple of reports from The Financial Times and TechCrunch today offer complementary details about a new wave of Apple threat notifications warning users that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware.

As we’ve covered before, Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to users it believes may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks. The company doesn’t disclose who may be behind the attacks or confirm whether a device has been compromised, but advises recipients to take the warnings seriously and seek expert assistance.

You can learn more about Apple’s recommendations for protecting against mercenary spyware, including how to enable Lockdown Mode, here.

Back to today’s reports, The Financial Times says that German lawmakers and government officials began receiving threat notifications from Apple last Thursday, prompting the country’s Federal Office for Information Security to issue an urgent warning over the weekend.

The agency advised recipients to “assume their device is no longer secure,” while the German government said it was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously” and “working flat out to investigate the circumstances of the incident.”

The FT noted that German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius declined to say whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those affected, and added that the attacks reportedly exploited a “zero-click” vulnerability, allowing attackers to compromise devices without any interaction.

Knowledge of their targets’ phone numbers was all that the hackers needed to carry out the attack.

As it reported on the alerts, TechCrunch noted that “others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple,” including Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, who shared his alert on X.

It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.

Mortada also noted in his tweet that he had previously been targeted by Pegasus spyware in 2017 and 2021, and that he does not know who was behind the latest attempt or whether it was connected to an investigative documentary he directed.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3535. SCOTUS sets hearing date for Apple’s appeal in Epic Games case

The U.S. Supreme Court has officially scheduled oral arguments in Apple’s appeal in its long-running legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Back in 2020, Epic Games sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store for introducing an alternative in-app payment system through a remotely activated update.

The following year, despite ruling in Apple’s favor on nine of Epic’s ten claims, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment options outside the App Store.

As a result, Apple changed its rules to allow external purchase links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them, along with restrictions on how those links could be presented.

Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, and the district court agreed. In April 2025, Judge Rogers ordered Apple to remove those restrictions and stop charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, finding the company in civil contempt for violating the original injunction.

Since then, Apple has allowed developers to direct users to external payment options in the US App Store without charging a commission, while continuing to challenge the contempt ruling.

After unsuccessful attempts before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, Apple eventually took its case to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to review whether Apple could be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction, even when its text did not specifically prohibit the conduct in question.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only review the civil contempt ruling, not how much, if anything, Apple can charge developers for purchases made outside the App Store. That issue is being handled separately by the district court, after the Ninth Circuit overturned the blanket ban on commissions in December.

Earlier today, the Supreme Court’s official docket for the case was updated with a date for oral arguments.

According to the filing, Apple and Epic Games will present their arguments before the Supreme Court on Monday, January 11, 2027, though both sides have already outlined many of their arguments in recent filings.

In September, Apple filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, arguing that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its brief, Apple cited multiple court decisions to support its argument that a party cannot be held in civil contempt unless an injunction clearly prohibits the conduct in question.

A few days after Apple’s filing, the US Department of Justice and several legal and business groups also submitted briefs supporting at least part of the company’s argument.

The DOJ, however, also argued that the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over some of its restrictions on external purchase links, including a requirement that developers use what Apple called “plain buttons,” which could not have contrasting backgrounds.

With the hearing now scheduled, the case is one step closer to a final decision from the Supreme Court. However, both sides still have some paperwork to submit before then, as Epic Games has until November 13 to file its brief responding to Apple’s arguments, while Apple’s reply is due December 14.

#3533. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3530. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3527. Apple earnings suggest the iPhone 18 launch strategy is really working

Yesterday’s AAPL earnings report revealed record revenue for a September quarter, and within it was an arguably even more significant record: iPhone revenue.

That’s because this year’s quarter only includes just two new iPhone models compared to the four released last year …

Apple reported fiscal quarter four revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year. Within that was iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, which was also a quarterly record. What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

What’s your take? Do you think it reflects well on iPhone 18 Pro sales, or do you think it can be explained away by the price increase and continuing popularity of the iPhone 17? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3524. How a Foot Injury & ‘Midlife Crisis’ Led to Kings of Leon’s ‘Therapeutic’ New Album ‘O My Beloved’

"It felt like something that I had buried down and hadn't really addressed," frontman Caleb Followill tells Billboard.

It was bad news when Kings of Leon frontman Caleb Followill broke his foot while playing tag with his children in spring 2025, forcing the group to cancel planned tour dates in the U.S. and Europe. Explore Kings of Leon See latest videos, charts and news

But the incident also provided the first step toward O My Beloved, the Grammy-winning Nashville quartet’s 10th studio album, out Friday (Nov. 6) on the group’s own Love Tap Records — a gentler and more reflective 13-song set that’s the first to be produced by the band itself. Related Queens of the Stone Age Crowned on ARIA Chart With 'Perfecth' Lil Baby Brings 'Fresh' to Life: Stream It Now Lil Baby, JENNIE, Dove Cameron, XG, Boys Noize & More: New Music Friday Guide

“That foot injury was a midlife crisis kind of deal,” says Followill, who formed Kings of Leon with his brother, drummer Nathan Followill, in 1999 (they were joined three years later by brother Jared and cousin Matthew Followill). “At first it was a lot of self-pity and also guilt, ’cause I felt like I was letting everyone down. After a little bit of that, I did grab the guitar and I started to play and the first thing that came out of that ended up being ‘My Whole World,'” O My Beloved‘s lead single.

“It just felt different,” Followill tells Billboard over Zoom. “I didn’t feel like I was writing something that I was necessarily going to put out into the world; it just felt therapeutic, and it felt like something that I had buried down and hadn’t really addressed. So that song came very naturally and very quickly. I just kept writing and the songs that came after that all had that same feeling.”

The tunes were decidedly not in the vein of most of the band’s catalog, including Billboard Hot 100 hits such as “Sex on Fire” and “Use Somebody,” even though Followill notes that “we have always had these moments on each of the albums where we bring it back to our roots, which is more songwriter-driven.” He expected that his new batch of material would be voted down and the troupe would go back to “the Kings of Leon thing which people expect to hear — the rock songs, the fast, up-tempo kind of stuff.”

To his surprise, however, that wasn’t the case.

“I was expecting to be met with a little hesitation, a little, ‘Let’s not try to switch up what people have come to expect,'” Followill recalls. “But it was the opposite. I feel like we’re all at the same place and we all felt like, ‘Yeah, it’s time to let the songs shine.’”

Working in its Neon Leon studio in Nashville, Followill says the group’s approach was “to feel the room that we were recording in.” That included sounds from trains rolling through a station across the street, which seeped into the recordings. “There’s trains all over the album,” he confirms. “You can hear a lot of walls rattling, but I think that adds something. It feels like a reverb or something.” He notes there was no thought of scrubbing that from the tracks.

“It’s not perfect, and we didn’t want it to be,” Followill explains. “We didn’t want bells and whistles. We didn’t want loud pedals and reverb and all the things that can make something sound better. We tried to avoid that. We just wanted the songs to shine.”

The result is an album that’s unlike anything else in Kings of Leon’s catalog. O My Beloved‘s songs are mostly mid-tempo and melody-forward, with an acoustic underpinning and careful nuances enhanced with strings, keyboards and hand percussion. Electric guitars — whether it’s the airy slides in “My Whole World,” the biting solo in “Cold Blue Dawn” or the soaring break in “Feel the Love” — embellish rather than the drive the tracks, making for an ambience that Followill says was wholly intentional in the process.

“Whatever we were playing, we wanted it to feel like a four-piece,” he notes. “At first we thought we were just making demos…but in the process, we would listen back and we were like, ‘I think this is better than demos.'” That, in turn, led to the decision for the band to produce O My Beloved itself.

“We felt like if we brought someone in, we were going to be fighting to make it sound like (it does), and we’re already getting there ourselves,” Followill explains. “We were just in our little paint factory, and the sounds we were getting were so authentic. We got to a place where it was like, ‘We don’t want anyone coming here. We want to do this ourselves. We want that challenge. We want to meet that opportunity.’ It was so freeing to have our own space and work on our own schedule and do things the way we wanted to do it.”

O My Beloved also takes a different lyrical bent — sentimental, philosophical and at times nostalgic, set off by occasional “threads of darkness” that represent the journey taken to the positive outlook that pushes through. At the same time, Kings of Leon end the album with Followill acknowledging “I think we still have a lot we’d like to learn” in “Get You Down.”

“I know we use the word gratitude a lot, but I don’t really know how else to describe it,” Followill says. “I felt like I was just looking back on our accomplishments, and outside of music — at our life and who we’ve become as men and fathers. There was a lot of appreciation and pride for that and the potential to continue doing what we do, because I feel like we’re at a place now where we love it more than we ever have.”

In addition to “My Whole World,” the group has advanced the album with the singles “KOYSAR” and “Cold Blue Dawn,” the latter accompanied by an inventive lyric video created with the Weather Channel using NASA satellite topography to spell out the words. The group will be in London for a show on Nov. 10 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 3. Australia is on tap for February and Europe for the summer.

A just-announced North American tour begins May 8 in Bristow, Va., and runs into early June, with a second leg during September and October. (See dates below.) And Followill predicts that the approach the band took on O My Beloved will make an impact on the rest of Kings of Leon’s repertoire.

“I feel like we can break our show up,” he says, “and maybe there are stripped-down versions of songs or a stripped-down set within the set. We’re still kinda working on it and playing with some fun (ideas); any chance we get to expand our sound, or even the opposite, those little challenges are exciting to us. We’ve played a thousand concerts; at this point we just want to have fun with it but also give people a great show when they come out.”

#3523. Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

What’s your take? Please share in the comments.

#3522. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3520. New iPad mini hands-on: Refreshed design, OLED display, more

Apple’s smallest iPad has gotten its biggest update in years. The new iPad mini features a much thinner and lighter design, a larger OLED display, water resistance, and the powerful A20 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing the new iPad mini, and there’s a lot to like — but also a couple of frustrations. Here’s everything you need to know.

The new iPad mini lives up to the “mini” name even more than its predecessor. It’s significantly thinner, down from 6.3mm on the previous iPad mini to 5.4mm on the new model. In fact, that puts it very close to the ultra-thin iPad Pro and the unfolded iPhone Duo. Here’s how it compares:

The new iPad mini is also significantly lighter, dropping from 293 grams to 255 grams. That puts it in the realm of the iPhone Duo, for comparison’s sake:

The reduction in weight and thickness was immediately noticeable when I picked up the new iPad mini. It feels significantly nicer to hold, more premium, and less “dense” in my hands.

The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch screen, a slight increase from the previous generation’s 8.3-inch display. The overall footprint is mostly the same (the new model is actually about 2.2mm narrower). The larger screen is possible because the new iPad mini’s bezels are 24 percent thinner than before.

In addition to allowing a bigger screen in the same form factor, the narrower bezels also modernize the iPad mini’s overall look and feel. The bezels are noticeably slimmer than the iPad Air and base model iPad, and slightly thinner than the iPad Pro.

With smaller bezels, a thinner chassis, and a lighter weight, the new iPad mini feels significantly more premium than before. It reminds me less of the base model iPad or iPad Air and more of the iPad Pro, just shrunken down.

The big news about the display, though, is the switch to OLED. This marks Apple’s first non-Pro iPad to offer an OLED screen. It’s not the fancy tandem OLED display of the iPad Pro, but it’s a huge improvement over the previous model’s LCD panel.

The new iPad mini offers SDR brightness up to 600 nits, up from the previous model’s 500 nits max. The iPad mini also supports HDR content, with up to 1200 nits peak brightness.

The new iPad mini’s screen is undeniably an improvement over its predecessor. All of the inherent benefits of OLED apply here, including better colors, improved contrast, higher brightness, and more.

Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind. Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.

Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering significantly faster pixel response time than the previous generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother scrolling and reduced motion blur.

I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages, scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher refresh-rate display.

I’m sure Apple knows the iPad mini’s market, and it seems to have decided not to prioritize ProMotion based on that information. However, as someone who has longed for a so-called “iPad mini Pro” for years, I’m disappointed by the decision. The new iPad mini’s screen is so much better … I just wish Apple had gone that extra step and added ProMotion. We’ve reached a point where ProMotion should be table stakes, especially after Apple brought it to the base iPhone 17 last year.

For an extra $100, you can upgrade the new iPad mini to have a nano-texture display (on the 256GB and 512GB models).

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s nano-texture display and have it on my 14-inch MacBook Pro. On the iPad mini, I think it makes even more sense.

The iPad mini is ultra-portable, and you naturally carry it around and use it in different lighting environments. The nano-texture glass helps reduce reflections and glare in a wide variety of lighting conditions. I also really like the combination of the iPad mini’s book-like size and the nano-texture finish.

There is a slight tradeoff in color vibrancy compared to a glossy OLED screen, as on other Apple devices with nano-texture, but it’s a very minor difference in my experience. The screen still looks fantastic.

One of the more interesting changes with the new iPad mini is something Apple calls the “Acoustic Display.” Instead of traditional speakers with visible grilles, Apple has developed a new system that uses the display itself to produce sound.

Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s significantly thinner design.

In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a test bed of sorts.)

The Acoustic Display also plays an important role in another major upgrade: water and dust resistance. The new iPad mini is IP67 rated, which means it can be immersed in 1 meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. It’s the first iPad to have an official water-resistance rating.

Adding water resistance to the iPad mini is particularly notable given its size and portability. I naturally find myself wanting to take it everywhere, and water resistance makes that more feasible.

One use case where all these improvements really come together is reading. The thinner and lighter design, nano-texture glass, and water resistance make the new iPad mini the most compelling iPad yet to serve as an e-reader.

The new iPad mini is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which I already covered in detail in my iPhone 18 Pro review. The short version: the A20 Pro chip gives you plenty of power for anything you can throw at the iPad mini today.

One detail worth calling out is that Apple uses two different versions of the A20 Pro in the iPad mini. The 128GB and 256GB models feature a five-core CPU and 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512GB model gets a six-core CPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. All three configurations feature the same seven-core GPU.

I don’t think anyone should buy the 512GB version of the iPad mini just for those extra cores. You should pick your iPad mini configuration based on how much storage you need, not the version of the A20 Pro chip. You don’t need to worry about performance with the new iPad mini. And perhaps most importantly, the A20 Pro chip ensures the iPad mini has enough headroom for the future.

There’s been a lot of consternation about where the iPad mini fits in a world where the iPhone Duo also now exists. It’s a fair question. After all, when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, the two devices share a similar form factor … but that’s really where the similarities end.

The iPad mini offers the full-fledged, unapologetic iPadOS experience. It supports the full multitasking prowess of an iPad Pro, including windowing and the menu bar. The new iPad mini also supports extended display mode, so you can plug it into an external display and extend your iPad experience there.

The iPad mini also gets iPadOS app layouts, and most importantly, a desktop-class browsing experience in Safari. It’s a remarkably capable device in a remarkably compact form factor. It fits where other iPads can’t, yet it runs the same version of iPadOS as other iPads.

The new iPad mini does all of that, but better than before. The thinner, lighter design paired with smaller bezels gives the new iPad mini a meaningful visual refresh. The added water resistance means you can do even more with the compact and pocketable iPad mini design.

But all of this comes at a higher price of $699. This marks the second price increase for the iPad mini this year. It started the year at $499, rose to $599 as part of Apple’s broader price increases in June, and is now $699 as of this refresh.

The new iPad mini also still starts with 128GB of storage. Increasing the base storage to 256GB would’ve helped ease some of the pain of that price increase. It’s also getting increasingly hard to manage a device with 128GB, particularly with the storage needs of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. The lack of ProMotion and Face ID also make the price increase sting more.

Ultimately, the iPad mini form factor is a joy to use. The design feels great in the hand, and having the full iPadOS experience in such a compact device remains impressive. It’s not quite the “iPad mini Pro” I’ve always wanted, but it’s big upgrade to a form factor that I’ve always loved.
